title: Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: Vieta jumping (olympiad technique) as a descent on certificates
connection: S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC has Vieta involutions B ↦ AC − B (and A ↦ (BC − A)… scaled by n). Vieta jumping descends any solution to a fundamental one, proving structure theorems (IMO 1988 Q6 style).
why: Vieta jumping is the elementary native tool for Markoff-type equations. It gives finite fundamental sets per (n, D) and transports positivity along orbits.
first_step: For n = p < 500, compute the fundamental (minimal) solutions under Vieta jumping on S_{p,D} and check whether ES certificates (2D | C) appear among fundamental solutions or in their orbits.

title: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak / W. Chen: Markoff mod p connectivity as a model for certificate graphs
connection: BGS proved strong approximation for Markoff surfaces mod p for most p; Chen proved the Γ-orbit of X*(p) is connected (divisibility of orbit sizes by p). ES surfaces have no comparable group action.
why: These are the nearest pointwise-for-all-p results on Markoff-type surfaces, and the precise reason they need a big group action. A hidden action on S_{n,D} would change the picture.
first_step: Search S_{n,D} (mod p) for additional birational automorphisms beyond Vieta (compute the automorphism group of the projective closure).

title: Ghosh–Sarnak integral Hasse failures for Markoff-type: count of k with failures as a calibration of ES-type counts
connection: Ghosh–Sarnak show many Markoff-type surfaces x²+y²+z²−xyz = k violate the integral Hasse principle, and that a positive proportion of k are not represented, beyond BM. ES's counts are of the same (log)² class-number scale.
why: It is a warning precedent: log CY with (log)² expected counts can fail infinitely often. ES survives verification to 10¹⁸, so any proof must use something Markoff lacks.
first_step: Compare the ES 'probability of zero' model with Ghosh–Sarnak's heuristics for Markoff numbers k; identify which structural difference makes ES failures not occur.

title: Composition on V_n as ideal multiplication in ℤ[2√f]: certificates as a 'box' in a narrow class group
connection: COMPOSITION_ES: V_n values at μ are the fibre over a fixed order-2 narrow class δ of the box of primitive ideals of norm dividing μ. ES ⇔ the box meets δ with an extra condition (B = 1).
why: Class-group 'boxes' (ideals of bounded norm generating/hitting a class) are a native class-field-theory question, with results via Bach's bound under GRH and unconditional Lamzouri-type results.
first_step: Calibrate: for μ in a window, size of box vs narrow class number; check whether GRH-Bach bounds would put the box onto δ (they handle generation, not hitting one class with norm constraints).

title: Heegner points / CM points equidistribution (Duke) for the lattice meeting point
connection: LATTICE_MEETING moves the slice inside Cl(−4p); Duke's theorem says CM points of discriminant −4p equidistribute on the modular curve. Certificates are CM points landing in a thin region (near the cusp, Y small).
why: Duke's theorem with explicit rates (Iwaniec's bound for half-integral-weight coefficients) is a pointwise-in-p existence statement for regions of size ≫ p^{−δ}. ES needs regions of size ≈ p^{−1/2}·polylog.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the 'certificate region' for CM points of disc −4p and compare with the best-known equidistribution error p^{−1/28}-type.
refs: Duke, Hyperbolic distribution problems and half-integral weight Maass forms (Invent. 1988)

title: Subconvexity for L(1/2, f × χ_{−4p}) and shrinking-target CM equidistribution
connection: Equidistribution of CM points in shrinking targets reduces (via Waldspurger) to subconvexity for twisted L-functions. ES certificates live in a target of measure ~p^{−1/2+o(1)}.
why: It gives the precise exponent gap: Weyl-strength subconvexity yields shrinking targets of size p^{−1/12}-ish, far from p^{−1/2}. It is a clean calibration.
first_step: Compute the target measure exactly, then the required subconvexity exponent; record the gap.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL₂ (Publ. IHES 2010)

title: Genus theory and the 2-part of Cl(−4p): ES sign as a genus character value
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), Cl(−4p) has 2-rank 1, and genus characters are (·/p) and χ_{−4}. Certificate ideals of norm e must lie in a principal genus or its complement; the slot lemma's mod-4 condition may be the 4-rank (Rédei) symbol.
why: Rédei symbols and 4-ranks are explicit and computable. If the ES sign is a Rédei symbol of the certificate ideal, the structure is governed by governing fields (Stevenhagen, Smith).
first_step: For p < 10⁵, compute the Rédei-matrix data of Q(√−p), Q(√−2p) and compare with p's ES₅ certificate statistics (sign distributions by level).
refs: Stevenhagen, Rédei reciprocity, governing fields and negative Pell (2018; check)

title: Negative Pell equation as a sibling: 'x² − py² = −1 always solvable for p ≡ 1 (4)' (Legendre) via parity
connection: Legendre's proof that x² − py² = −1 is solvable for primes p ≡ 1 (4) is a pointwise existence proof from a parity/descent argument on the fundamental unit. It is the classic pointwise thin existence at primes ≡ 1 (4).
why: ES's hard primes are p ≡ 1 (4). A Legendre-type argument (the unit's norm is ±1 and +1 leads to a contradiction via factorisation) is the cleanest (R)-rigidity precedent at exactly these primes.
first_step: Write Legendre's argument abstractly (a factorisation of ε − 1 forces a divisor equation with no solution) and look for the analogous ES 'unit' (e.g. in ℤ[√p] or ℤ[√(tp+1)]).

title: Fermat two-squares via Thue's lemma (pigeonhole) as a template for ES at primes ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Thue: given ρ² ≡ −1 mod p, pigeonhole gives x ≡ ρy with |x|,|y| < √p, hence p = x² + y². ES's lattice L_ρ(g) uses ρ² ≡ −p mod g, a Thue-type lattice; certificates are short vectors with extra divisibility.
why: It is the most elementary pointwise prime theorem from a thick object (lattice of covolume p). ES needs the short vector to hit a divisor condition, which is where pigeonhole breaks.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice-point condition as 'a short vector of L_ρ(g) lies in a sublattice of index k' and compute the pigeonhole threshold vs the actual vector lengths.

title: Quaternion order Λ_{d,m}: reduced-norm representation of p by a ternary sublattice
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.2: Λ_{d,m} = ℤ⟨u,v⟩ with u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1 is an order. Type I data are elements of prescribed norm/trace. ES becomes 'p is represented by a specific ternary norm form attached to (d,m)'.
why: Representation by ternary forms attached to orders has a theory: Gross lattices, Eichler orders, spinor genera. A family over (d,m) gives many forms, any of which suffices.
first_step: For each (d,m) ≤ 20 compute the Gross lattice (trace-zero part) and its genus; check whether p's representability by that genus is automatic (local conditions only) and whether spinor exceptions arise.

title: Spinor-exceptional integers as an analogue of T1 squares
connection: Ternary forms can fail to represent integers in whole square classes t·m² (spinor exceptions; Schulze-Pillot, Earnest–Hsia). T1 kills ES certificates at odd squares. Both are square-class phenomena from a quadratic obstruction.
why: Spinor-exception theory classifies exactly which square classes fail, and proves representation outside them for large n. If T1 is a spinor exception, the 'outside' theorem suggests ES-type existence.
first_step: Test whether T1's empty square classes coincide with spinor-exceptional square classes of a ternary form attached to certificates (Λ_{d,m} Gross lattice) for small d,m.
refs: Schulze-Pillot, Exceptional integers for genera of integral ternary positive definite quadratic forms (Duke 2000)

title: Siegel–Weil formula for the certificate genus: average over the genus is the BM main term
connection: Siegel–Weil: the genus-averaged representation number is a product of local densities, i.e. an Eisenstein coefficient. BM's main term is exactly such a product. The difference from a single class is a cusp-form coefficient.
why: In the quadratic-form toolbox, pointwise lower bounds come from 'Eisenstein main term ≫ cusp error'. ES's analogue has main term log²p, too small for cusp bounds; this is the native statement of the B3 obstacle.
first_step: Compute the ratio of BM main term to the trivial cusp-form bound in the best available quadratic encoding (rank 4, QUATERNION_ES); record the exponent gap.

title: Borcherds products / divisors of automorphic forms with zeros at CM points
connection: A Borcherds product has explicit divisor supported on Heegner/CM points. If ES failure at p corresponded to a CM point where some form must vanish, the Borcherds lift might prohibit it.
why: It is the native 'existence via zeros of modular functions' tool, with exact divisor formulas. Speculative but categorically meaningful.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/bsC_valence_borcherds.md for the prior attempt; identify which weakly holomorphic input (principal part) would encode certificate data.
refs: Borcherds, Automorphic forms with singularities on Grassmannians (Invent. 1998)

title: Tunnell-type criterion: a ternary-form count whose vanishing ⇔ ES failure
connection: Tunnell expresses the congruent number property, conditionally on BSD, via the difference of counts of two ternary forms (via Waldspurger). An ES analogue would be an identity N₋(p) = (count of form Q₁) − ½(count of Q₂)-type.
why: It is the textbook example of a sign/existence problem translated exactly to ternary-form counts. SIGN_IDENTITY rules out holomorphic forms by size, but a Tunnell-shaped identity for a related 0/1 quantity (not the full count) is not excluded.
first_step: Search for ternary forms Q₁,Q₂ with det ∝ 4·2^k whose representation counts at p correlate with the indicator [λ(p) ≤ 3] or with N₋(p) mod 2.
refs: Tunnell, A classical Diophantine problem and modular forms of weight 3/2 (Invent. 1983)

title: Dedekind eta multiplier and the ES sign: (A/p) as an eta-multiplier value on γ_w
connection: The eta multiplier ε(γ) is given by Dedekind sums, and Rademacher's formulas relate it to Jacobi symbols. The ES sign is the theta multiplier on γ_w (bsB_theta_multiplier), and θ and η multipliers are related (θ = η⁵/(η²η²)-type identities).
why: Expressing the sign via η multipliers gives a conjugacy-invariant (Rademacher Φ function / class invariant), which might be easier to sum over words.
first_step: Compute Rademacher's Φ(γ_w) for words at p < 1000 and check whether Φ mod 8 or 24 determines the sign.

title: Rademacher symbol Φ(γ) = linking number of the modular knot with the trefoil (Ghys)
connection: Ghys: for hyperbolic γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), Rademacher's Φ(γ) equals the linking number of the closed geodesic (modular knot) in SL₂(ℝ)/SL₂(ℤ) = S³ − trefoil with the trefoil. If the ES sign is a function of Φ(γ_w), it becomes a linking number.
why: A topological meaning for the sign would bring knot-theoretic positivity/counting (Ghys's theorem) to ES; at least it is an exact dictionary.
first_step: Compute Φ(γ_w) for words (from the cutting sequence) and test whether Φ mod 4 determines the slot-lemma sign.

title: Hilbert modular / Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles for the pair (A, A*) with AA* = tp+1
connection: Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles T_N on Hilbert modular surfaces have intersection numbers given by class numbers. Pairs (A,A*) with AA* = tp + 1 are points of a 'norm' condition that might be intersection points of T_N with a modular curve.
why: Hirzebruch–Zagier gives exact intersection numbers as coefficients of modular forms; if certificates are intersection points, their count is a known modular coefficient.
first_step: Check whether pairs (A, A*) with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t) and AA* = tp+1 are naturally CM points / intersection points on X(1) × X(1) (i.e. on a Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1}).
refs: Hirzebruch–Zagier, Intersection numbers of curves on Hilbert modular surfaces (Invent. 1976)

title: Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1} on X(1) × X(1) and ES words as its points with level structure
connection: Pairs of lattices with cyclic isogeny of degree N_t = tp+1 form the modular curve X₀(N_t). A word is a factorisation N_t = A·A* with congruences mod t, which is a Γ₀/Γ₁-level datum.
why: It gives ES₅ a moduli interpretation: level-t structures on isogenies of degree tp + 1. Moduli-theoretic counts (Riemann–Hurwitz on X₀) are exact.
first_step: Write the bijection {words of level t} ↔ {points on a specified cover of X₀(N_t) over ℤ}; check whether the sign is a Galois/Atkin–Lehner action.

title: ES is a Π⁰₁ sentence: consequences for independence and proof strength
connection: Positive solutions obey explicit bounds (x ≤ 3n/4 and polynomial bounds on y, z), so ES ⇔ ∀n ∃(bounded) x,y,z: a Π⁰₁ statement. If ES were independent of PA, it would be true.
why: This is the logic-native calibration: ES cannot be 'true but unprovable-without-counterexample' in a way that makes it false. It also means any proof can in principle be checked by bounded search per n (no Σ-complexity).
first_step: Write the precise bounds (Curtiss/ET) and state ES as a Π⁰₁ formula; check whether 'almost all n' (Vaughan) is formalisable in IΣ₁.

title: Bounded arithmetic: is the Mordell covering (ES for n ∉ hard classes) provable in IΔ₀ + Ω₁?
connection: Bounded arithmetic proves elementary NT statements whose witnesses are polynomial-time computable. ES for the easy residue classes has explicit polynomial witnesses (Mordell identities), so it is provable in very weak systems.
why: Proof-complexity calibration: a proof of full ES in a weak system would yield a polynomial-time witness algorithm (Buss witnessing). Conversely, if no poly-time deterministic witness algorithm exists, any proof must use strong axioms or non-constructive steps.
first_step: State the witnessing theorem consequence: ES provable in S¹₂ ⇒ a poly-time algorithm outputs (x,y,z) from n. Check whether any deterministic poly-time ES algorithm is known (likely not without factoring).

title: TFNP classification: ES-SEARCH and the parity (PPA) / pigeonhole (PPP) classes
connection: Assuming ES, 'given n, output (x,y,z)' is a total search problem. A windmill/parity proof would put it in PPA, a pigeonhole proof in PPP, a potential/descent proof in PLS. Fermat two-squares (Zagier windmill) is the canonical PPA-type number-theoretic search.
why: Complexity theory gives a vocabulary for the kind of non-constructive argument a proof could use. Proving ES-SEARCH lies in some class by an explicit reduction is a proof of ES.
first_step: Write the WINDMILL.md reduction (weighted parity of solutions) as a PPA instance template; check whether any known PPA-complete problem (e.g. 'Leaf') has a natural ES-shaped instance.
refs: Papadimitriou, On the complexity of the parity argument (JCSS 1994)

title: Deterministic polynomial-time ES algorithm as an equivalent target ('constructive ES')
connection: A polylog-time certificate search with a proof of termination is ES plus an algorithm. Randomised factoring-based searches succeed heuristically in polylog trials. Derandomisation theory (hitting sets for structured sets) is the native frame.
why: Hitting-set constructions for 'divisor-in-class' events are a computational-complexity lens: an explicit small set of levels C guaranteed to contain a working one is exactly a pointwise theorem.
first_step: Measure, for p ≤ 10⁹ (repo data), the smallest universal family of levels covering all tested p; compare with hitting-set size lower bounds from the Mordell–Schinzel obstruction (any finite family fails).

title: Existential theory of (ℕ, +, |) (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov) and fixed-C Type II statements
connection: At a fixed level C, 'p has a certificate' is ∃d,k: d | 4Cp+1 ∧ d = 4Ck − 1, an existential formula in (ℕ,+,|) with parameter p. Lipshitz proved the existential theory of (ℤ,+,|) decidable; the ∀p∃ fragment is a different matter.
why: It locates the logical complexity of finite-menu ES statements. A decidable ∀∃ fragment would make 'ES via levels C ≤ C₀' algorithmically decidable, although B1 says such statements are false.
first_step: Check the literature on the decidability of ∀∃ sentences of (ℕ,+,|) (Bel'tyukov, Lipshitz); record whether multiplication becomes definable there.
refs: Lipshitz, The Diophantine problem for addition and divisibility (Trans. AMS 1978)

title: Lean/Mathlib formalisation of the reduction chain and of T1 as an infrastructure item
connection: Formalising Mordell's reduction to the hard classes, the ES₅ ⇒ ES implication, the slot lemma and T1 in Lean gives a machine-checked map. The AI+Lean pipeline solved several Erdős problems in 2025–26.
why: It does not prove ES, but it provides a verified testbed for candidate lemmas and makes automated search over proof shapes possible.
first_step: Check Mathlib/Formal Conjectures for an existing ES statement (Google DeepMind formal-conjectures repo has Erdős problems; check whether ES is #242 there); formalise the slot lemma first.

title: SAT/SMT encoding of 'p has no certificate up to level C₀' to find structural UNSAT cores
connection: Encode 'no word/certificate with parameters ≤ B at prime p' as a SAT/SMT instance (bit-vector arithmetic). UNSAT cores for many p might reveal which constraints jointly force existence.
why: SAT cores are a native discovery tool for finite combinatorial obstructions. They might expose a small set of congruence facts that always produces a certificate (or show none exists, B1).
first_step: Encode for fixed p ~ 10⁴ with bounded parameters in Z3; extract UNSAT cores of 'ES₅ fails' across 100 primes and compare them.

title: Legendre PRF security as a 'cryptographic hypothesis' implying ES₅ for all large p
connection: The Legendre symbol PRF (Damgård) is conjectured to be pseudorandom. ES₅ failure at p means (·/p) is identically +1 on the efficiently enumerable set S₃(p) (size ≈ log²p). A uniform family of such failures would be a distinguisher.
why: It translates ES₅ into crypto language: infinitely many failures form a 'weak key' class. Crypto hardness assumptions are heuristic and asymptotic, so this gives density, not all p.
first_step: Formalise: 'for all poly-size circuits C enumerating sets S_p ⊂ F_p, Pr_p[χ_p|S_p ≡ 1] ≈ 2^{−|S_p|}'; check which crypto literature (Legendre PRF attacks: Khovratovich; Beullens et al.) bounds such events.
refs: Damgård, On the randomness of Legendre and Jacobi sequences (CRYPTO 1988)

title: Quadratic residue codes: ES₅ failure as S₃(p) ⊂ support of the QR idempotent
connection: The QR code of length p is defined by the QR set. ES₅ fails at p iff S₃(p) ⊆ QR. Coding theory studies which structured sets sit inside QR (e.g. minimum-weight words, automorphism group PSL₂(p) acting on QR codes).
why: The QR code's automorphism group PSL₂(F_p) is large. Words (as SL₂ data) act naturally, so S₃(p) ⊆ QR might be translated into a code-automorphism statement.
first_step: Check whether S₃(p) is a union of orbits of some subgroup of PSL₂(F_p) stabilising QR; if so, failure would be forced or forbidden group-theoretically.
refs: MacWilliams–Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes, ch. 16

title: Gauss-sum / Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃(p)} at the quadratic character
connection: ES₅(p) ⇔ Σ_{A ∈ S₃(p)} (A/p) < |S₃(p)|. In coding/Fourier terms, the quadratic Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃} must not be maximal. Uncertainty principles (Tao's prime-field uncertainty, Biró–Meshulam) bound how concentrated a set and its Fourier transform can be.
why: Tao's uncertainty principle for F_p says |supp f| + |supp f̂| ≥ p + 1. Indicator sets that are subsets of QR have structured Fourier transforms, which gives a potential contradiction with S₃'s known Fourier structure.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform of 1_{S₃(p)} for p < 5000; check whether 'S₃ ⊆ QR' would force a Fourier property contradicted by S₃'s divisor structure.
refs: Tao, An uncertainty principle for cyclic groups of prime order (MRL 2005)

title: Lovász Local Lemma (constructive Moser–Tardos) for building a counterexample-free menu, and its dual
connection: The LLL shows existence of objects avoiding many weakly dependent bad events. For ES, the bad events are 'level C fails at p', and the LLL (or its converse, Shearer's bound) quantifies when all failing is possible.
why: It is the probabilistic-method native tool for 'all events fail simultaneously'. A Shearer-type obstruction would show that failure configurations at a fixed p are inconsistent.
first_step: Model level failures at fixed p as events in a dependency graph indexed by shared prime factors of 4Cp+1; compute the Shearer region for p < 10⁶ data.

title: Janson/second-moment for the certificate count at fixed p
connection: N(p) = Σ_C Σ_{d} 1[d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)]. The second-moment method gives P(N(p) = 0) ≤ Var/E². Janson's inequality handles positively correlated events. Both need pairwise dependence controlled at fixed p.
why: It is the textbook route to existence of rare objects. At fixed p there is no randomness, so this only works with a pseudo-random model of factorisations, as EXSET_ARITH_JANSON did.
first_step: Re-read EXSET_ARITH_JANSON_*.md; record the exact place where the fixed-p model needs an unproved independence.

title: Random multiplicative function model of (·/p) on divisor-generated sets (Harper's low moments)
connection: Model (·/p) restricted to S₃(p) by a random multiplicative function f. Then ES₅ failure is 'f ≡ 1 on a structured set'. Harper showed better-than-square-root cancellation for Σ f(n) (low moments), so multiplicative structure reduces fluctuations.
why: It is the native probabilistic model for character values with multiplicative constraints; it gives a heuristic failure probability that respects multiplicative dependencies among elements of S₃(p).
first_step: Compute the multiplicative dependency rank of S₃(p) (dimension of the F₂-span of its exponent vectors over primes). The failure probability under the model is 2^{−rank}; compare with observed.
refs: Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I (Forum Math Pi 2020)

title: F₂-linear algebra: ES₅ failure ⇔ a linear system over F₂ in the Legendre symbols of small primes
connection: (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q(A)}. ES₅ failure ⇔ all A ∈ S₃(p) have Σ v_q(A)·ε_q ≡ 0 (mod 2), where ε_q = [(q/p) = −1]. This is a linear system over F₂ in the unknown vector ε (the 'quadratic character of p on primes').
why: The exact linear-algebra form shows that failure is consistent iff the exponent-vector matrix of S₃(p) has the actual ε in its right kernel. Rank considerations give a sharp combinatorial necessary condition.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ compute rank_F₂ of the exponent matrix of S₃(p) (over primes dividing elements) and the codimension of the failure space; record the minimum over p.

title: Statistical-mechanics partition function over all ES solutions and Lee–Yang zeros
connection: Define Z_n(β) = Σ_{solutions} (xyz)^{−β}. ES(n) ⇔ Z_n ≢ 0. Lee–Yang-type theorems locate zeros of partition functions with ferromagnetic structure. A family Z(n, β) analytic in n-related variables might have provably non-vanishing coefficients.
why: Speculative, but it is the stat-mech native form of 'nonempty'; the Dirichlet series Σ_n Z_n(β) n^{−s} is a height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰.
first_step: Compute the height zeta function Σ_n Σ_{sol} n^{−s}(xyz)^{−β} numerically; check for Euler-product structure.

title: Height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰 and its analytic continuation
connection: Σ_{(n,x,y,z) ∈ 𝒰(ℤ_{>0})} H(n,x,y,z)^{−s} counts all ES solutions. Its rightmost pole gives the log²-order average count (ET). Its analytic structure, e.g. as a sum of Eisenstein-type series via the torsor, is native to Manin-conjecture methods (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel).
why: Analytic continuation gives secondary terms, which control the lower tail in short intervals of n, a step towards almost-all-with-rates.
first_step: Write the height zeta function via ET's parametrisation as a multiple Dirichlet series and identify its polar structure.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics (2010)

title: Large deviations / lower-tail of the certificate count: Poisson vs Gaussian regime
connection: The certificate count N(p) has mean ≍ log²p. P(N(p) = 0) is a lower-tail large deviation. In random-graph theory (Janson–Łuczak–Ruciński) lower tails are governed by Janson's inequality and are exponential in the mean.
why: The lower-tail exponent ≈ mean gives P(0) ≈ p^{−c log p}, summable over p: ES true heuristically. Native LDP theory would quantify the needed dependence structure.
first_step: Fit log P(N = 0 | mean M) from data (repo has it) against the Janson prediction −M/(1+Δ/M); record Δ.

title: Branching-process / tree-search model of the certificate search (Galton–Watson survival)
connection: Searching levels C = 1,2,… and divisor splits gives a search tree; the probability of finding no certificate is an extinction probability of a branching process with offspring ~ divisor counts.
why: Branching processes give exact extinction-probability equations, which give a sharper heuristic than Poisson when certificates cluster.
first_step: Model the per-level offspring distribution from data; solve the extinction equation and compare with observed zero frequencies for ES₅.

title: Percolation on the forest F_p: giant component reaching a QNR
connection: If F_p behaves like a random graph above the percolation threshold, the component of 1 is giant and contains a QNR. ES₅ (p ≡ 1 mod 8) follows from 'the component of 1 contains a QNR'.
why: Percolation-native: thresholds are sharp, and arithmetic graphs (divisor graphs) have percolation results (e.g. random divisor graphs). The forest might be supercritical in a window of small vertices.
first_step: Compute the degree distribution and component structure of F_p restricted to vertices ≤ X for p < 10⁷; locate the effective percolation threshold.

title: Maker–Breaker / Erdős–Selfridge criterion for covering-system strategies
connection: View 'adversary chooses p's residues prime by prime, prover covers with certificates' as a Maker–Breaker game on a hypergraph of congruence certificates. The Erdős–Selfridge criterion Σ 2^{−|e|} < 1/2 gives Breaker (adversary) a win.
why: It turns B1 (no finite covering) into a game-theory calculation and might quantify how large the certificate hypergraph must be for a covering, compared with the actual size.
first_step: Compute the Erdős–Selfridge potential of the certificate hypergraph up to level C₀ (edges = residue-class conditions on p); see where it crosses 1/2.

title: Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé / model-theoretic: nonstandard counterexample prime and Loeb measure
connection: If ES fails for infinitely many primes, an ultrapower contains a nonstandard prime P with no certificate. Loeb measure on S₃(P) and nonstandard divisor counts give a 'limit object' whose properties are constrained by transfer.
why: Nonstandard analysis turns 'infinitely many failures' into 'one hyperfinite failure', where measure-theoretic tools (e.g. Furstenberg correspondence) apply.
first_step: Formulate the hyperfinite failure object and see whether a known ergodic-theoretic theorem (via a correspondence principle) contradicts it. Likely only density results, but record.

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view of the sporadic lists (U(n) and Rickards–Stange-type exceptions)
connection: Finite sporadic lists in local-global problems (U(n): six values; RS: 15) have low Kolmogorov complexity only if explained by structure. An algorithmic-information test can flag 'structured' vs 'random' sporadics.
why: Exploratory: a compressible sporadic list suggests a hidden obstruction that might also act at primes.
first_step: Factorisations (computed): 105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, 3985 = 5·797, 25305 = 3·5·7·241, 111969 = 3³·11·13·29, 978145 = 5·7·27947. All are ≡ 1 (mod 8); mod 840 they are 105, 441 = 21², 625 = 25², 105, 249, 385, so two lie in square classes mod 840. Next: test whether every sporadic lies in a class mod 840·k that is 'square-like' for U's local model.

title: Machine-learned certificate selectors: features that predict the first working level
connection: Train a classifier on p ↦ least working level (or least u in I3_𝒞), with features such as Legendre symbols of small primes, p mod small moduli and factorisations of p+small. Interpretable models (sparse logistic, decision trees) may expose a structure.
why: This is the data-science native lens. Many repo results (I3_𝒞 u ≤ 39) suggest the selector is simple; a sparse rule could be a conjecture or a lemma candidate.
first_step: Using repo data for p ≤ 10⁹, fit a depth-6 decision tree predicting the least certifying u in I3_𝒞 from (q/p) for q ≤ 50; report accuracy and the tree.

title: Garsia–Milne involution principle for a bijective ES-count identity
connection: The involution principle builds a bijection from two sign-reversing involutions. If N₋(p) = (count of a simple positive set) − (count of another) via explicit involutions, Garsia–Milne yields a bijection and hence positivity whenever the simple set is bigger.
why: It is the enumerative-combinatorics native machine for turning signed identities into injections. Positivity of ES would follow from an injection from a set of known size ≥ 1.
first_step: Look for any signed identity for N₋ (SIGN_IDENTITY lists the known ones); check whether its terms are counts of explicit finite sets amenable to involutions.

title: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot: words as non-intersecting lattice path families with determinant tuv−u−v
connection: det M(t,u,v) can be read as a signed count of path systems in a planar network (LGV). If the planar network can be chosen so that the count is non-negative termwise, the cofactor A and its class get a path interpretation.
why: LGV gives combinatorial meaning to determinants and cofactors, the same objects as the ES sign (cofactor A mod p). Positivity of path counts is automatic.
first_step: Construct the planar network whose LGV matrix is M(t,u,v); interpret A = tu−1 as a path count and the slot-lemma 4-divisibility as a parity/symmetry of path families.

title: Kasteleyn/Pfaffian orientations: ES count as a Pfaffian of a skew matrix built from p
connection: Perfect matchings of planar graphs are Pfaffians. Windmill-type 'odd number of fixed points' arguments are mod-2 Pfaffian/determinant arguments. A planar graph G_p with ES certificates as matchings would give #certificates = |Pf(K_p)|.
why: Exact Pfaffian formulas give closed-form counts, and nonvanishing of a determinant is checkable algebraically (e.g. via its value mod a prime).
first_step: Attempt to realise the forest F_p's edges or the words as perfect matchings of a planar graph; compute det mod 2 for small p.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over F₂ for a parity count of certificates
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives #solutions ≡ 0 (mod p) for low-degree systems over F_p; integer analogues count solutions mod 2 via polynomial identities. INVOLUTION_ES / WINDMILL ask for an odd weighted count of ES solutions.
why: It is the algebraic native parity tool. It applies to finite-field point counts, not positive integer points, unless the certificate set is encoded as F₂-points of an auxiliary variety.
first_step: Encode the slot-lemma condition (4 | some pentagon entry) as F₂-variety points of an auxiliary system over (ℤ/2)^k (via binary digits?) and compute counts mod 2 for p < 2000.

title: Smith theory / ℤ/2-equivariant topology: fixed points of an involution on a ℤ/2-acyclic certificate complex
connection: Smith theory: an involution on a mod-2 acyclic finite complex has a non-empty mod-2 acyclic fixed set. A simplicial complex on solutions (or near-solutions) that is provably ℤ/2-acyclic, with an involution whose fixed points are certificates, would give existence.
why: It is the topological generalisation of 'odd number of fixed points', more flexible than plain parity because acyclicity can be proved by shellability or discrete Morse theory.
first_step: Define a complex on words of all p′ ≤ p (or on near-certificates) with faces from shared letters; compute mod-2 homology for small p.

title: Discrete Morse theory / matching on the poset of near-solutions
connection: Acyclic matchings on a poset (Forman) count critical cells, and Euler characteristic = alternating count of critical cells. If an ES-defined poset has Euler characteristic ≠ 0, a critical cell (certificate) must exist.
why: It is a combinatorial-topology tool that generalises sign-reversing involutions with a global acyclicity condition, a strictly richer version of the windmill route.
first_step: Define a poset of partial certificates (e.g. levels/divisor pairs ordered by divisibility) and compute its Euler characteristic as a function of p (small p).
refs: Forman, Morse theory for cell complexes (1998)

title: Lefschetz number of a map on a 'certificate space' with ES-certificate fixed points
connection: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem: L(f) ≠ 0 ⇒ fixed point. A continuous or algebraic self-map of a compact space whose fixed points are ES certificates and whose Lefschetz number is computable would prove existence.
why: It is the classic topological existence engine; the windmill is its discrete special case. A finite-field version (Lefschetz trace for Frobenius) counts points over F_q, not integral points.
first_step: Record the attempts in invol_topological.md; look for algebraic maps on U_n's compactification whose fixed loci are positive points (e.g. the cyclic permutation composed with a birational involution).

title: Sperner / KKM / Tucker lemmas for a labelled triangulation whose 'rainbow cell' is a certificate
connection: Sperner's lemma gives an odd number of fully labelled simplices. If the triangle {x+y+z = const} or the (u,v) quadrant can be triangulated with labels from p-arithmetic (e.g. Legendre symbols and divisibility), a rainbow cell might encode a word with the right sign.
why: It is the combinatorial-topology native parity engine with geometric flexibility. The forest bichromatic-edge statement is already a 1-dimensional Sperner-type statement (path from QR to QNR has a bichromatic edge).
first_step: Write the 1-D Sperner argument behind H4/forest bichromatic edges explicitly; then look for a 2-D labelling that encodes the extra divisibility.

title: Borwein–Choi's xy+yz+zx theorem as the closest proved sibling of I3/U(n)
connection: Borwein–Choi: there are at most 19 integers not of the form xy+yz+zx (x,y,z ≥ 1). Eighteen are known, and the 19th is excluded under GRH. The form is classified via class groups of Q(√−n), using (x+z)(y+z) = n + z². I3 is n = tuv−u−v ⇔ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1.
why: It is structurally parallel (a factorisation of n + (shift) with constraints) and is proved up to one possible exception via idoneal-type class-number arguments. The I3/U analogue would be 'finitely many failures, all but one effective'.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and translate: for which discriminants does 'tn+1 has no factorisation (tu−1)(tv−1)' force a class-group condition (exponent ≤ 2) on Q(√−?)?
refs: Borwein–Choi, On the representations of xy+yz+zx, Exp. Math. 9 (2000) 153–158

title: Class-number-one-type ineffectivity: is I3's exceptional list finite by a Siegel-type argument?
connection: Chowla proved finiteness of idoneal numbers via Siegel's (ineffective) class-number bound. If I3 failure at n forced a large class group to have a small exponent (an 'idoneal-type' condition), Siegel–Tatuzawa would give finiteness of exceptions up to one.
why: It is the only known mechanism turning a 'polylog-witness' representation problem into a pointwise theorem (with ineffectivity). It is the (R)-rigidity type of FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Look for a map: I3 failure at n ⇒ the class group of some order of disc −D(n) has exponent ≤ 2 (or bounded); test on the known I3 exceptions.
refs: Chowla, An extension of Heilbronn's class-number theorem (1934)

title: Lorenzini's critical-polynomial question (W) and the A₃ graph: I3 as a sandpile statement
connection: LORENZINI_W: (W) asks that every n outside a finite set is xyz − x − z (x,y,z ≥ 2), which comes from critical groups of A₃-type graphs. I3 (t,u,v ≥ 3) is a strengthening.
why: This is the graph-theory native home of I3. Lorenzini's and Wang–Lu's density-1 results are its nearest theorems.
first_step: Check Wang–Lu (EJC 2026) methods for density 1 and whether they extend to the I3 lower bound t,u,v ≥ 3 (repo has an unconditional rate).
refs: Wang–Lu, The critical polynomials of simple connected graphs, EJC 33(3) (2026)

title: Bloom's density theorem for unit fractions as a 'thick-set' Egyptian result
connection: Bloom proved that any set of positive upper density contains a finite S with Σ_{s∈S} 1/s = 1 (Erdős–Graham density conjecture); Croot proved the colouring version. ES is a three-term, fixed-numerator, thin version.
why: It is the nearest proved Egyptian-fraction existence theorem. Its method (Fourier analysis on smooth numbers) needs many terms; recording it calibrates the term-count axis.
first_step: Check whether Bloom's method proves '4/n is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators in a prescribed dense set' for bounded k, and what k it needs.
refs: Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions (Ann. Math. 2003)

title: Egyptian fractions with restricted denominators (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang) and ES variants
connection: Results on representing rationals with denominators from restricted sets (odd, squarefree, from an AP) give variants. 'ES with odd denominators' or 'ES with denominators ≡ r mod m' are sibling statements with their own local obstructions.
why: Sibling failures/successes calibrate which constraints the T1 obstruction interacts with.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.6118 and arXiv:1606.02117; tabulate which three-term restricted variants of 4/n are known false and true.

title: Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n as a family: uniform-in-m translation
connection: The m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z conjectures (Schinzel: for n ≥ n₀(m)) share U_n's geometry with 4 replaced by m. T1-type obstructions should exist at m-dependent square classes.
why: A translation that works for all m simultaneously (e.g. a fibration over m) might reveal which part of ES is specific to 4.
first_step: Compute the analogue of T1 for m = 5, 6, 7 (which square classes kill the standard certificate lines) and compare with the known hard classes for Sierpiński's 5/n.

title: Covering systems (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba): why Mordell's coverings must stop
connection: Hough's minimum-modulus theorem and the BBMST distortion method give structure theorems on covering systems. ES's 'cover all primes by polynomial identities' is a covering by sets that are not plain residue classes (square classes are excluded).
why: Distortion-method techniques bound the density covered by systems with large moduli. An ES-specific version would quantify the B1 barrier precisely.
first_step: Apply the BBMST distortion bound to the family of Mordell-type certificate classes up to modulus M; compute the uncovered density lower bound.
refs: BBMST, The Erdős–Selfridge problem with square-free moduli (2019; check)

title: Function-field ES: Weil-bound positivity as the model where pointwise ES is provable
connection: Over F_q[T], ES-type statements have proved variants (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*). The native reason is that Weil's RH gives square-root cancellation in short character sums, which is unavailable over ℤ.
why: It records the 'what does RH give' calibration: whether ES_q holds for all P of large degree by Weil bounds, and which step uses RH for curves.
first_step: Re-read FUNCTIONFIELD_ES3 / FF_STERILE_* for the exact proved statements and the step where the Weil bound enters; state the ℤ-analogue hypothesis needed.

title: Drinfeld modules / Carlitz module: ES_q certificates as torsion points
connection: DRINFELD_ES: degree-k Diff-parity over F_q(T) via rank-k Drinfeld modules. Carlitz torsion gives cyclotomic function fields where Frobenius of P is explicit.
why: In function fields, 'divisor of 4CP+1 in a class' is a Chebotarev statement in Carlitz cyclotomic extensions, with effective Chebotarev (Weil). This is the native tool.
first_step: State the function-field Type II at fixed level C as a Chebotarev condition in F_q(T)(Λ_{4C}) and compute the effective error.

title: Large-q limit (Katz–Sarnak) of the ES_q certificate count distribution
connection: As q → ∞ with deg P fixed, counts of certificates become equidistributed statistics governed by monodromy groups (Katz's equidistribution). The probability of zero certificates in the limit is computable.
why: It gives an exact 'random model' limit of the ES count distribution, a rigorous analogue of the Poisson heuristic, and possibly a proof of ES_q for q large relative to the degree.
first_step: Identify the monodromy group of the certificate-counting sheaf (divisor-in-class conditions) and compute the limiting P(count = 0) for small degrees.
refs: Katz–Sarnak, Random Matrices, Frobenius Eigenvalues, and Monodromy (1999)

title: Power ladder ES_(k): cubic and higher rungs collapse to finite coverings
connection: POWER_LADDER_ES: for odd k, ES_(k) (third denominator a k-th power) is a finite congruence covering mod 4, while even k returns to ES^□. The native field is power-residue symbols and Waring-type coverings.
why: Calibration item: it shows exactly which relaxations are trivially true. A new rung (e.g. denominators in a norm group of a cyclic field) can be tested the same way.
first_step: Generalise: third denominator in N(K^×) for an abelian field K; find the index condition that makes the rung a finite covering.

title: I3 at 2^k ± 1 by exponent coverings: Sierpiński-number technique
connection: I3 holds on 2^k ± 1 etc. by exponent coverings (I3_DEEP). This is exactly the Sierpiński/Riesel-number covering technique for k·2^n + 1 compositeness.
why: Covering congruences in the exponent are a native tool that is complete for its families. Extending to 'n = a·b^k + c' families tests how far exponent coverings go.
first_step: Try families n = 3^k ± 2, 5·3^k + 1 with exponent coverings for I3; record which ones close.

title: Additive basis view of I3: tuv−u−v as a 'thin basis' of order 1 with three free parameters
connection: The set W₃ = {tuv − u − v : t,u,v ≥ 3} has counting function ≍ N (it is almost everything), but the representation function is only ≍ log²n. Thin-basis theory (Erdős–Tetali; Nathanson) studies bases with small representation functions.
why: Erdős–Tetali gives random bases with r(n) ≍ log n that are bases for all large n. Deterministic thin bases with full coverage are rare; I3 would be a natural deterministic example.
first_step: Survey known deterministic 'thin bases' with polylog representation functions and full coverage; check whether any proof technique applies to multiplicative shapes.
refs: Erdős–Tetali, Representations of integers as the sum of k terms (1990)

title: Goldbach-type circle method for I3? The minor arcs for tuv − u − v
connection: The circle method treats additive representations. I3 is multiplicative-additive (tuv − u − v), so its exponential-sum generating function Σ e(α(tuv−u−v)) factors through divisor sums. The major arcs give the local density (Haar survival).
why: It gives the analytic-NT native attempt and shows the minor-arc problem is like the ternary divisor problem in progressions (d₃ in APs), which has level of distribution results (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown).
first_step: Write the singular series for I3 and compare with I3_DEEP's Haar survival; record the minor-arc bound needed for a pointwise result (polylog main term ⇒ impossible).

title: Erdős #306-type Fourier counts (Li 2609.32140) and why abundance is needed
connection: Recent AI/Lean-assisted solutions of Erdős problems (e.g. Li's #306) use Fourier counts over exponentially many configurations. ES has polylog witnesses.
why: Calibration: these tools apply to ES variants with many more terms (k ≥ log n unit fractions). They locate the minimal k where Fourier methods work.
first_step: Find the smallest k(n) for which '4/n is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ n^C' is provable by a Fourier count; compare with k = 3.

title: Greedy / Engel / Sylvester expansions as dynamical systems on rationals
connection: The greedy (Fibonacci–Sylvester) algorithm and Engel/Pierce expansions are dynamical maps on ℚ ∩ (0,1). ES asks for a 3-step orbit-like decomposition, not necessarily greedy.
why: Odd greedy and other algorithms have termination theorems and counterexample families. An algorithm with provable 3-step termination on 4/p would prove ES.
first_step: Test 'greedy with a bounded look-ahead' algorithms (choose x among the first K candidates ≥ ⌈p/4⌉) for 3-term termination at all p < 10⁸; find the minimal K(p) growth.

title: Unit-fraction graph on ℚ: 3-step walks from 0 to 4/n
connection: Define the graph on ℚ_{>0} with r ~ r + 1/k. ES(n) ⇔ dist(0, 4/n) ≤ 3. Farey neighbours a/b, c/d satisfy c/d − a/b = 1/(bd), so unit steps between Farey neighbours are edges.
why: It gives a metric-geometry view of Egyptian fractions. Bounds on the graph's diameter on {m/n : m ≤ 4} are exactly ES-type statements, and 'every m/n at distance ≤ c·log log n' results are known.
first_step: Compute the distance-2 neighbourhood of 4/p (pairs 1/y + 1/z) and its overlap with {4/p − 1/x}; record which Farey structure produces most certificates.

title: Fractional quantum Hall hierarchy: the chain matrix as a K-matrix and the ES sign as an anyon-theory class
connection: Haldane–Halperin hierarchy states have tridiagonal K-matrices whose filling is an HJ continued fraction. The anyon theory is the discriminant form of K on ℤ^r/Kℤ^r (here ℤ/p). ES₅(p) ⇔ a 3-level hierarchy state with det K = p whose ℤ/p anyon braiding form is in the non-square class.
why: Abelian Chern–Simons theory classifies anyon theories with ℤ/p fusion into two classes (by the Gauss sum and chiral central charge). Physics constraints such as Gauss–Milgram relate the class to the signature and to spin structure.
first_step: Write the topological spins θ_x = e^{πi x²A/p} for the fan K-matrix; compute the Gauss–Milgram sum (odd/fermionic version) and relate it to the slot lemma.
refs: Wen, Quantum Field Theory of Many-Body Systems ch. 7 (K-matrix)

title: Slot lemma as a van der Blij / Gauss–Milgram formula for odd lattices (characteristic covectors)
connection: For an odd lattice, the Gauss sum of the discriminant form is governed by σ − w² mod 8, where w is a characteristic covector (van der Blij, Brown invariant). For the chain lattice, w has coordinates (v,t,u) mod 2 and w² has denominator p. This plausibly yields (A/p) as a function of p mod 8 and the parity pattern of (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. the slot lemma.
why: It would give the slot lemma a structural (lattice-theoretic) proof and a generalisation to chains of any length, i.e. an exact sign rule for λ(p) ≤ L words.
first_step: Compute σ − w² mod 8 symbolically for the 3-chain and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all parity classes of (t,u,v) mod 8; then do the 4-chain.
refs: van der Blij, An invariant of quadratic forms mod 8 (1959)

title: q-deformed rationals [p/A]_q (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links
connection: MGO's q-rationals have numerator polynomials with positive coefficients, which equal (up to normalisation) Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links (Kogiso–Wakui). The fan graph is the Tait graph, so the Jones polynomial is a Tutte specialisation. ES₅ concerns the class of A, i.e. which 2-bridge link has numerator p.
why: A root-of-unity specialisation detecting (A/p) would make the ES sign a quantum invariant with positivity structure (q-rationals), possibly giving inequalities.
first_step: Compute [p/A]_q numerators for p < 300 and evaluate at q = i, e^{iπ/4}, e^{2πi/8}; test whether any evaluation's phase equals (A/p) on words.
refs: Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko, q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions (Forum Math. Sigma 2020; check)

title: Tutte polynomial of the fan graph: evaluations beyond T(1,1) = p
connection: The fan multigraph's Tutte polynomial T(x,y) has T(1,1) = p. Other evaluations count forests, acyclic orientations, recurrent sandpile levels (Merino) and, via Thistlethwaite, the Jones polynomial of the associated alternating link.
why: It is a single polynomial carrying graph, sandpile and knot data. The ES sign might be an evaluation (e.g. T(−1,−1) or a root-of-unity value).
first_step: Compute T(x,y) symbolically for the fan in terms of (t,u,v) and evaluate at small roots of unity; correlate with the slot-lemma sign.

title: ES₅ words as integral points of a twisted M₀,₅ (A₂ cluster variety = M₀,₅)
connection: The A₂ cluster variety is M₀,₅ (configurations of 5 points on P¹), and positive integral friezes correspond to special integral points. The coefficient-N pentagon is a twist/deformation. Integral points of M₀,₅ over ℤ[1/S] are governed by S-unit equations.
why: This brings the S-unit equation toolbox (finiteness, effective bounds, counting) and the cross-ratio coordinates of M₀,₅ to ES₅ words.
first_step: Write the five frieze entries as cross-ratios of 5 points on P¹ and identify the N-twist; check whether words correspond to points of M₀,₅ with cross-ratios in a multiplicative set related to N.

title: Pentagon identity of the dilogarithm on the coefficient-N pentagon
connection: The Rogers dilogarithm satisfies the 5-term relation along A₂ mutations: Σ L(X_i/(1+X_i)) = π²/2 on the positive real locus. With frozen coefficient N the relation acquires N-dependent terms. Words give rational points.
why: Dilogarithm identities encode K₂/Bloch-group data of the points. For rational points, Bloch-group elements are torsion, which gives exact identities; the sign might appear as a torsion class.
first_step: Compute Σ L over the five X-coordinates of each word for p < 100 numerically; look for a pattern in N and in the sign.

title: Stern's diatomic sequence: (p, A) = (s(k), s(k+1)) and HJ length as a binary-run statistic of k
connection: Every coprime pair occurs exactly once as consecutive Stern values, and the CF of p/A is encoded by the run lengths of k's binary expansion. ES₅ ⇔ some k with s(k) = p, s(k±1) ≡ non-residue, and k's binary word in a 3-run HJ pattern.
why: This makes ES₅ a statement about binary words, so automata/regular-language tools (automatic sequences, Stern's sequence is 2-regular) apply.
first_step: Find the exact HJ-run encoding (LORENZINI_W §7 has a Stern coding); enumerate k with ≤ 3 HJ-runs and s(k) = p, check the sign.

title: Commute time / escape probability on the fan: A/p as a random-walk quantity
connection: For the fan graph, R_eff(a,s) = A/p, so the commute time between a and the sink is 2|E|·A/p and the escape probability from a is 1/(v·R_eff) = p/(vA). The ES sign is a residuosity property of a commute time numerator.
why: Random-walk interpretations allow coupling/monotonicity arguments (Rayleigh monotonicity: adding edges decreases resistance), which could organise words by a partial order.
first_step: Use Rayleigh monotonicity to order words of p by resistance; check whether the sign changes monotonically along chains (data p < 10⁵).
refs: Doyle–Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks (1984)

title: Hilbert basis of a 2-dimensional cone: ES₅ ⇔ a cone of index p in the non-residue class with a 5-element Hilbert basis
connection: The Hilbert basis of cone((0,1),(p,−A)) consists of the HJ convergents, so it has r(p/A) + 2 elements. ES₅ ⇔ some cone of type 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has Hilbert basis of size 5.
why: Integer-programming/commutative-algebra native: Hilbert-basis sizes and normal semigroup rings (embedding dimension). Toric-ideal theory gives explicit invariants.
first_step: Compute the semigroup-ring invariants (Hilbert series, a-invariant) of the 5-element cones and test whether the sign is a ring-theoretic invariant (e.g. class group element of the toric ring).

title: Divisor class group of the toric ring k[σ^∨ ∩ M] ≅ ℤ/p and the canonical class: the sign as an Atiyah–Bott/Gorenstein index datum
connection: The cyclic quotient 1/p(1,A) has class group ℤ/p generated by a boundary divisor D₁. The canonical class K corresponds to −(1 + A)·[D₁]-type data, so the 'position of K in ℤ/p' is a quadratic-residue question about 1 + A or A.
why: Native singularity invariants (Gorenstein index, canonical class position) are computable and might rephrase the sign as 'K is a square multiple of a generator'.
first_step: Compute [K] ∈ Cl = ℤ/p for 1/p(1,A) and express its square class via A; compare with (A/p).

title: Arithmetic topology (Morishita): Legendre symbol as mod-2 linking number of prime knots
connection: In arithmetic topology (q/p) is the mod-2 linking number of 'prime knots' p and q in Spec ℤ. (A/p) = Σ_q v_q(A) lk(p,q) mod 2, and Rédei symbols are Milnor triple-linking numbers. ES₅ asks p to link oddly with the 'certificate link' of some word.
why: The dictionary might suggest topological constructions (Seifert surfaces = genus-theory objects) that force an odd linking. Speculative, but categorically sound.
first_step: Read Morishita, Knots and Primes ch. 4–8; translate the slot lemma into linking-number language and see whether a Seifert-surface argument suggests a certificate.

title: Multiplicative generation of F_p^* by forest edge products
connection: A = (p+u)/v ≡ u/v (mod p), so (A/p) = (uv/p) on forest edges. ES₅ fails ⇒ every edge product uv lies in the QR subgroup ⇒ the group generated by edge products is ≠ F_p^*. So ES₅(p) ⇐ 'edge products generate F_p^*'.
why: Generation of (ℤ/q)^× by small structured sets is now proved for almost all q (Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen). Edge products are small integers with a divisibility constraint; this links ES₅ to the 'small sets generate' literature.
first_step: Compute the index of ⟨uv : (u,v) edge of F_p, u,v ≤ X⟩ in F_p^* as X grows, p < 10⁶; compare the least X needed with the least QNR.

title: s-form: ES(p) ⇔ ∃ s ∈ ℕ³ with lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i, S) = p (value of an arithmetic function)
connection: GEOMETRY_ES: positive points ↔ primitive s with 4s_i | nS, and ES(p) ⟺ ∃ s with m(s) = lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i,S) = p. ES says the arithmetic function m on primitive triples hits every prime.
why: Surjectivity of an explicit arithmetic function on ℕ³ is the native form for additive/multiplicative combinatorics (value sets of lcm/gcd expressions, like the problem of values of lcm(a,b)/gcd(a,b)-type maps).
first_step: Compute the distribution of m(s) over s ≤ B and the smallest-height s with m(s) = p for p < 10⁶; look at the gcd(4s_i, S) pattern of minimal solutions.

title: Fair-division reading (Rhind papyrus): 4 loaves among n people, each share as 3 distinct unit fractions
connection: ES(n) ⇔ 4 loaves can be split among n people so that each share is exactly three unit-fraction pieces. This is the historical Egyptian 2/n-table problem generalised.
why: It is a pure restatement, recorded once. It suggests looking at the scribes' algorithms (choose the first denominator from n's divisors-plus-offset), which match Type I/II choices.
first_step: Compare the Rhind 2/n table's rules with Type I/II certificate selection rules (historical algorithms as certificate selectors).

title: Positivstellensatz / SOS degree of infeasibility certificates for bounded ES failures
connection: For bounded parameters, 'no certificate at p up to height B' is a finite infeasibility statement with a Positivstellensatz/SOS (or Nullstellensatz) refutation. The degree needed as a function of p and B is a proof-complexity measure.
why: If refutation degree must grow, low-degree 'algebraic' proofs of existence are impossible in a quantifiable sense (analogue of B1). If it stays bounded for some encoding, that encoding has hidden structure.
first_step: For p failing ES₅ at small B (e.g. p = 5, 13, 17, 2521 for I3_𝒞), compute minimal Nullstellensatz degree over F₂ of the bounded infeasibility system.

title: Lucas-sequence primitive divisors (Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier) as a source of prime divisors ≡ −1 (mod m)
connection: Primitive prime divisors q of U_m(P,Q) satisfy q ≡ (D/q) (mod m), so q ≡ −1 (mod m) when (D/q) = −1. ES Type II needs a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1. If 4Cp+1 shares a primitive divisor with a suitable U_{4C}, the certificate follows.
why: BHV give existence of primitive divisors for all m > 30, a pointwise rigidity theorem. The question is whether p-dependent Lucas sequences can be tied to 4Cp+1.
first_step: Look for Lucas parameters (P,Q) depending on p with 4Cp+1 | U_{4C}(P,Q)·(small) for some C; test small p by search.
refs: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (Crelle 2001)

title: Sum of two squares p = a² + b² and the Hecke-angle of p vs ES-hardness
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 (4) have a Gaussian angle θ_p (p = a² + b²). Hecke Grössencharacters equidistribute θ_p. If ES-hardness (e.g. large least certificate level, or λ(p) large) correlated with θ_p, ES would interact with ℤ[i]-arithmetic.
why: It is cheap and tests whether the Gaussian structure that p ≡ 1 (4) brings carries ES information. A null result rules out a class of approaches.
first_step: For p < 10⁸, correlate min certificate level / λ(p) / N₋(p) with θ_p and with a mod small numbers.

title: Quartic residue symbol (A/p)₄ on certificates: hidden finer obstruction?
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), the quartic symbol refines (A/p). If certificates' quartic symbols are biased (e.g. never i for some class of p), there may be a finer reciprocity structure, as in the Apollonian quartic obstruction.
why: Quartic reciprocity obstructions appeared in HKRS for Apollonian packings. A quartic bias in ES certificates would be a new invariant.
first_step: Compute the distribution of (A/p)₄ over all ES₅ words with (A/p) = −1 for p ≡ 1 (8), p < 10⁶.

title: Erdős–Kac jointly over levels: dependence of ω(4Cp+1) across C via shared small primes
connection: Level failures are dependent because 4Cp+1 and 4C′p+1 share small prime factors when C ≡ C′ mod q-structures. The joint distribution of (ω(4Cp+1))_C is a Kubilius-model question.
why: It quantifies how independent the per-level events are, the input any probabilistic or sieve approach needs.
first_step: Compute empirical correlations of 1[level C fails] across C ≤ 50 for p < 10⁷ and fit a Kubilius-type model.

title: Khinchine flatness theorem for convex pieces of the certificate region
connection: A convex body with no lattice points has bounded lattice width (Khinchine flatness). The hyperbolic certificate region splits into convex pieces, so if ES fails at p, every convex piece is lattice-free and thin in some lattice direction.
why: Flatness-type arguments are the geometry-of-numbers native way to derive structure from emptiness. Here 'thin in a direction' might contradict the known shape of the region.
first_step: Take the region {(X,Y): XY ≈ tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t)} in the lattice of those congruences; compute convex pieces' widths and compare with flatness constants.

title: Banaszczyk transference / covering radius for BALANCED_LATTICE relation lattices
connection: BALANCED_LATTICE uses μ_∞(Λ) (covering radius) of relation lattices of small primes mod q. Banaszczyk's transference theorems tie covering radius to dual minima, and the dual minima correspond to characters that are nearly trivial on S.
why: It is the lattice-theory native tool and is already partly used; recorded for completeness. Sharper transference (Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz) could improve constants.
first_step: Check whether the R–SD reverse Minkowski / transference improvements change BALANCED_LATTICE's numerical thresholds.
refs: Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz, A reverse Minkowski theorem (Ann. Math. 2024; check)

title: Lattice-based crypto SIS/LWE hardness as a heuristic for certificate existence in relation lattices
connection: The relation lattice Λ_q(S) = {x : ∏ g_s^{x_s} = 1} is an SIS-type lattice. Its short vectors relate to subset products hitting targets. Crypto worst-case to average-case reductions say random such lattices have short vectors of predictable length (Gaussian heuristic).
why: Gaussian-heuristic predictions for short vectors give a model of certificate existence that respects lattice structure, more refined than Poisson.
first_step: Compare the Gaussian heuristic for λ₁(Λ_q(S)) with actual values for q < 10⁵, S = first k primes; quantify the deviation.

title: Hecke (Rosen) continued fractions: ES-type statements for Hecke triangle groups G_q
connection: Replace SL₂(ℤ) by the Hecke group G_q and HJ fractions by Rosen λ_q-fractions. 'Every element of a cusp set has a length-3 expansion with a character condition' becomes a family of ES-analogues indexed by q.
why: Some Hecke groups are arithmetic (q = 3, 4, 6) and others non-arithmetic. Comparing ES analogues across them separates arithmetic from combinatorial ingredients.
first_step: Define the λ₄-analogue (G₄ is commensurable with Γ₀(2)) of words and check whether a T1-type obstruction occurs.
refs: Rosen, A class of continued fractions associated with certain properly discontinuous groups (Duke 1954)

title: Fermionic/spin TQFT: the parity condition '4 divides an entry' as a spin-structure obstruction
connection: In 3-manifold topology, spin structures on L(p,q) and plumbings are tracked by characteristic sublinks (Wu sets). 'Some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4)' may say the plumbing admits a spin structure with a given Rokhlin invariant mod 16.
why: Rokhlin's theorem (σ ≡ 0 mod 16 for spin closed 4-manifolds) is a rigid integrality statement. If the ES sign is a Rokhlin invariant, T1 might be a Rokhlin-type obstruction.
first_step: Compute μ-invariants (Neumann–Siebenmann) of L(p,A) via plumbing for all words with p < 500 and compare with the sign.
refs: Neumann, An invariant of plumbed homology spheres (1980)

title: Integrable billiards / Sturmian cutting sequences of slope A/p in a square
connection: A billiard trajectory in the unit square with slope A/p has a cutting sequence (Sturmian/Christoffel word). HJ length is a renormalisation depth (number of Rauzy–Veech-type induction steps of a specific kind).
why: Rauzy–Veech induction is the dynamics-native renormalisation, and it has a version for square-tiled surfaces where arithmetic data (p) enters as the number of squares.
first_step: Identify HJ steps with a renormalisation algorithm on the square torus; check whether a square-tiled surface with p squares realises words as cylinder decompositions.

title: Square-tiled surfaces with p squares: cylinder decompositions ↔ words
connection: Origamis (square-tiled surfaces) with p squares have cylinder decompositions with heights, widths and twists satisfying Σ h_i w_i = p. A 3-cylinder decomposition with parameters (t,u,v)-type could encode tuv − u − v = p and the sign as a monodromy-group property.
why: Origami monodromy groups (subgroups of S_p) have classifications. 'Monodromy contains an odd permutation' style conditions are Legendre-type (Zolotarev: (A/p) is the sign of x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p).
first_step: Using Zolotarev's lemma, (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax mod p. Look for an origami with p squares whose horizontal/vertical permutations are x ↦ x+1 and x ↦ Ax, and whose cylinder structure encodes the word.

title: Zolotarev: (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p — ES₅ as 'an odd multiplication permutation with a length-3 HJ structure'
connection: (A/p) = sgn(π_A), π_A(x) = Ax mod p. ES₅(p) ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) gives an odd permutation. Permutation-group language: the parity of π_A can be computed from the cycle type (order of A in F_p^*).
why: (A/p) = −1 ⇔ ord(A) is even with the full 2-part of p−1, i.e. A generates the 2-Sylow quotient. So ES₅ becomes a statement about the 2-adic valuation of multiplicative orders of elements of L₃(p).
first_step: For p ≡ 1 (8), compute v₂(ord_p(A)) for A ∈ L₃(p); ES₅ ⇔ some A has v₂(ord A) = v₂(p−1). Look at the distribution of v₂(ord A) on words.

title: Artin-type: elements of L₃(p) with maximal 2-part of order; links to Artin's conjecture methods
connection: ES₅ ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) has v₂(ord_p A) = v₂(p − 1). Artin-type problems (Heath-Brown, Gupta–Murty) prove that one of a few fixed integers is a primitive root mod infinitely many p. Here the candidate set depends on p.
why: It translates ES₅ into the language of multiplicative orders, where Chebotarev in Kummer extensions Q(ζ_{2^k}, A^{1/2^k}) is the native tool, but A depends on p (B2).
first_step: Check whether a fixed-A family (e.g. A = 2·3 − 1 = 5 from the word (2,3,v)) with v₂(ord_p 5) = v₂(p−1) covers a Chebotarev set of primes, and compute its density.
refs: Heath-Brown, Artin's conjecture for primitive roots (1986)

title: Fixed-letter word families as Chebotarev sets: density of p covered by words with (t,u) fixed
connection: Fixing (t,u) makes A = tu − 1 fixed, and the word exists iff v = (p+u)/A is an integer, i.e. p ≡ −u (mod A). The sign condition (A/p) = −1 is then fixed by reciprocity: given p ≡ −u (mod A) and p mod 4, (A/p) = ±(−u/A) is determined. So each fixed (t,u) covers either a whole residue class mod 4A of primes or nothing (that is, it is the Mordell/B1 structure).
why: It is the cleanest 'fixed-menu' native form, and B1 says finitely many never suffice. The densities and their union bound give the exact covering deficit in Chebotarev language.
first_step: Compute the union density of fixed-(t,u) families with tu ≤ T as T grows (inclusion–exclusion via CRT), and the rate at which the uncovered density decays.

title: Weil representation of SL₂(ℤ/4p) and the sign as a matrix coefficient
connection: The theta multiplier is the Weil representation's character on Γ₀(4). The ES sign on γ_w is a matrix coefficient of the Weil representation of SL₂(ℤ/4p) (finite group). Representation theory of finite groups gives orthogonality relations for such coefficients.
why: Summing a matrix coefficient over a subset of the group equals an inner product. If the word set were a union of double cosets, orthogonality would give exact counts.
first_step: Reduce {γ_w} mod 4p and test whether it is (close to) a union of double cosets of a small subgroup (e.g. the Borel); compute the sign sum via characters.

title: Parity barrier (Selberg) check: is ES's sign condition a parity-sensitive sieve problem?
connection: Selberg's parity problem prevents sieves from distinguishing integers with an even or odd number of prime factors. The ES sign (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q} is a 'twisted parity' of A's factorisation, which suggests sieve methods face a parity-type barrier.
why: It is the sieve-theory native diagnosis. Repo PARITY_AUDIT may cover it; the twisted-parity framing via (·/p) might be new.
first_step: Check PARITY_AUDIT.md; formalise the 'twisted parity' barrier: construct a weight that agrees with sieve axioms but kills (A/p) = −1 terms.

title: Brown–Rödl partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y = 1/z and inhomogeneous colourings
connection: Brown–Rödl: in every finite colouring of ℕ the equation 1/x + 1/y = 1/z has a monochromatic solution. Croot: 1 = Σ 1/x_i monochromatic. ES is inhomogeneous (4/n), but 'colour n by ES status' and look for monochromatic structures.
why: Ramsey-theory native: a hypothetical ES-failure set F cannot contain configurations forced by partition regularity of related equations, which gives structural constraints on F.
first_step: Find equations E with E(n₁,…) ∧ ES(n₁) ∧ … ⇒ ES(n_k) (transport laws) and combine them with partition regularity to constrain F's structure.
refs: Brown–Rödl, Monochromatic solutions to equations with unit fractions (Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 1991)

title: Transport laws as a semigroup action: ES failures form a set closed under 'inverse transport'
connection: ES(m) ⇒ ES(km) trivially, and the repo has transport laws between different n. The failure set F is downward-closed under divisibility (if ES(n) fails then ES(d) fails for all d | n). Order theory: F is an order ideal in (ℕ, |).
why: Order-ideal structure plus density-zero (Vaughan) gives constraints, e.g. F ∩ primes determines F. Translating richer transport laws into a semigroup acting on ℕ gives an algebraic object (orbit closures).
first_step: List all proved transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md, DELTA_TRANSPORT.md) as maps n ↦ f(n). Compute the semigroup they generate and its orbits on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Conway's rational tangles: p/A as a tangle fraction and HJ length 3 as a 3-twist tangle
connection: Conway's rational tangles are classified by their fraction p/A, and tangle operations (twist, rotate) act as SL₂(ℤ)/PSL₂ moves. ES₅ asks for a 3-twist-region tangle (in the plumbing/even sense) whose fraction's denominator is a non-residue mod p.
why: It gives a diagrammatic calculus for words where 'sum of tangles' corresponds to Farey-sum-type operations, a potential source of composition laws between words.
first_step: Express the word (v,t,u) as a tangle word; check whether tangle sum (numerator closure of T₁ + T₂) maps ES₅ words of p₁, p₂ to words of p₁p₂-related numbers.
refs: Conway, An enumeration of knots and links (1970)

title: Pseudosquares (Lehmer; Williams–Sorenson) as the native list of ES-hardest primes
connection: T1 kills certificates at odd squares. Primes that are locally square-like (≡ 1 mod 8 and QR modulo all small primes) should be hardest. Lehmer's pseudosquares L_q (least non-square ≡ 1 mod 8 that is a QR mod all primes ≤ q) are tabulated far beyond 10¹⁸. Note 2521 = 2520 + 1, the last I3_𝒞 zero, is ≡ 1 modulo every integer ≤ 10.
why: Pseudosquare tables give an explicit list of the 'most square-like' integers, where an ES failure would be most likely; testing ES/ES₅/I3_𝒞 there is a targeted stress test beyond 10¹⁸.
first_step: Take the known pseudosquares and pseudosquare primes (Sorenson's tables up to ~10²⁵); run the ES certificate search on each; record certificate level and count vs nearby primes.
refs: Williams–Sorenson / Sorenson, 'The pseudosquares prime sieve' (ANTS 2006; check)

title: Rav's two-term criterion: ES ⇔ ∃x, two divisors of nx summing to 0 mod (4x−n)
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is solvable iff there are divisors d₁, d₂ of b with a | d₁ + d₂ (Rav 1966). With a/b = (4x−n)/(nx), ES(n) ⇔ ∃ x ∈ (n/4, n/2]-ish and divisors d₁, d₂ | nx with (4x − n) | d₁ + d₂.
why: It turns ES into additive combinatorics of divisor sets modulo m = 4x − n: 'the divisor set D(nx) satisfies D + D ∋ 0 mod m'. Sumset tools (Cauchy–Davenport, Kneser) are native.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and each x, check whether |D(px) mod m| is large enough that Kneser/Cauchy–Davenport would force 0 ∈ D + D (mod m), and how often that alone certifies.
refs: Rav, On the representation of rational numbers as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions (Crelle 1966)

title: Kneser's theorem on D(px) + D(px) mod (4x − p) and its stabiliser
connection: If 0 ∉ D + D (mod m), Kneser gives |D + D| ≥ 2|D| − |H| for the stabiliser H. Divisor sets of px are multiplicatively structured (D(px) = D(p)·D(x)), so the additive stabiliser is likely trivial, giving a size condition.
why: It is the cleanest additive-combinatorics translation of 'certificate exists at x'. Only size and structure of D(x) mod m enter.
first_step: Compute, over x, the ratio |D(px) mod m|/m; find the x where 2|D| > m (Cauchy–Davenport forces D + D = ℤ/m when m is prime). Record whether such x exist for all p.

title: Braid group B₃ lift of γ_w and link invariants of its closure
connection: SL₂(ℤ) is a quotient of B₃ (B₃ → SL₂(ℤ), kernel generated by (σ₁σ₂)⁶). Lifting γ_w to a braid and closing gives a link L_w. Link invariants (signature, Jones at roots of unity) are then functions of the word.
why: It gives another topological carrier of words, different from the 2-bridge/plumbing one, with Burau/Jones machinery.
first_step: Lift γ_w via M(b) ↦ σ₁^b σ₂^{−1}-type words; compute the signature of closures for p < 200 and compare with the sign.

title: Torus bundles T_{γ_w}: H₁ order |tr γ_w − 2| and Anosov dynamics
connection: The mapping torus of γ_w on T² has H₁ = ℤ ⊕ coker(γ_w − I) with |coker| = |tr γ_w − 2| = tu + tv − 4. Its linking form and Sol geometry are explicit.
why: A 3-manifold carrier where the trace, not p, is the order. The ES sign may appear as a linking-form class at a different modulus, which gives a new dictionary for transport between p and traces.
first_step: Compute the linking form of T_{γ_w} for words at p < 300 and look for a relation between its square class and (A/p).

title: Shioda's Mordell–Weil lattices: integral points of the ES elliptic fibration as small-height sections
connection: On a rational elliptic surface, integral sections (polynomial points) are exactly sections of small height in the Mordell–Weil lattice (Shioda). The plane-section fibration of the ES cubic gives an elliptic surface, and positive integer points restricted to fibres are its integral points.
why: MW lattices are explicitly computable (E₈-type root lattices for rational elliptic surfaces). Polynomial ES families (Mordell identities) would correspond to minimal-norm sections.
first_step: Compute the MW lattice of the x+y+z = s fibration of the ES cubic over Q(n)(s); list minimal sections and compare with Mordell identities.

title: Weak del Pezzo of degree 3 from the nodal ES cubic: Weyl-group orbits of the 9 lines
connection: The minimal resolution of the closure is a weak del Pezzo surface of degree 3 whose (−2)-curves form a root system. The Weyl group of the complement acts on lines/conic bundles. GEOMETRY_ES records 9 rational lines.
why: The lattice-theoretic structure (Pic ≅ I_{1,6}, roots) organises all conic fibrations, i.e. all 'Type I/II-like' families, in one Weyl orbit picture.
first_step: Compute the root system of the nodes and the orbit structure of conic classes; list the conic fibrations defined over ℚ and match them to known certificate types.

title: Exceptional triples and the B₃ braid action: Markov-type invariant vs S_{n,D}
connection: Exceptional collections of 3 objects have Gram matrices [[1,a,b],[0,1,c],[0,0,1]], and the braid group acts by mutations preserving a² + b² + c² − abc (Bondal–Polishchuk). S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC is a weighted variant, like a non-symmetric (n-twisted) category.
why: A categorical source of mutations for S_{n,D} would give the missing infinite group action (cf. BGS/Chen), and categories come with positivity (dimension vectors).
first_step: Check whether weighted Gram matrices [[1,a,b],[0,n,c],[0,0,1]]-type (objects with End of rank n) give the invariant nA² + B² + D − ABC under a braid action.
refs: Bondal–Polishchuk, Homological properties of associative algebras: the method of helices (1993)

title: Mod-p relaxation: depth-3 products in SL₂(F_p) generated by M(b) and Helfgott growth
connection: Modulo p, tuv − u − v ≡ 0 allows words of kp for any k. In SL₂(F_p), the set X = {M(b) : b ∈ F_p} grows: X·X·X is large (Helfgott, Bourgain–Gamburd). This is the mod-p relaxation of ES₅ (losing the archimedean size condition).
why: It isolates the archimedean condition (tuv − u − v = p exactly) as the whole content, a sharp calibration: the algebraic mod-p problem is easy, and the size cut is hard.
first_step: Record the mod-p statement: for each p, does M(v)M(t)M(u) ≡ upper-triangular-with-sign have solutions with t,u,v small? Find the smallest letter bound needed vs p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL₂(ℤ/pℤ) (Ann. Math. 2008)

title: Poisson–Dirichlet model for the factorisation of 4Cp+1 and subset-product coverage of −1
connection: Large prime factors of a random integer follow the Poisson–Dirichlet(1) law (Billingsley). Combining it with uniform classes of factors in (ℤ/4C)^× gives an exact model probability that no divisor is ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: It gives a principled per-level failure probability, which can be aggregated over levels with the correlation structure.
first_step: Simulate PD(1) factorisations with random classes for C ≤ 30; compare P(fail) with empirical per-level failure for 4Cp+1, p < 10⁸.
refs: Billingsley, On the distribution of large prime divisors (1972)

title: Character-orthogonality formula: level failure ⇔ Σ_χ χ(−1) ∏_{q^e‖N}(1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) = 0
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ −1 (mod m)} = φ(m)⁻¹ Σ_{χ mod m} χ(−1) ∏_{q^e‖N} Σ_{j≤e} χ(q)^j. Level failure is the vanishing of this non-negative sum, an identity in the characters' values at N's prime factors.
why: It is the harmonic-analysis native form; the sum is a 'multiplicative energy' quantity. Vanishing requires massive cancellation among characters, which might be impossible when N has a factor in a 'generic' class.
first_step: Characterise exactly when the sum vanishes for ω(N) ≤ 3 (finite group computation); this classifies per-level failure patterns.

title: Eisenstein's lattice-point proof of reciprocity applied to Σ_{words} (A/p)
connection: Eisenstein proves reciprocity by counting lattice points under a line. The sign of a word reduces by reciprocity to (−t/A)-type symbols, and Gauss's lemma turns these into lattice-point parities. Summing over words gives a lattice-point count in a region bounded by hyperbolas and lines.
why: A lattice-point expression for N₊ − N₋ would make the sign sum a geometry-of-numbers object with possible exact evaluation.
first_step: Write (A/p) for A = tu − 1 via Gauss's lemma as (−1)^{#lattice points}; sum over words for small p and look for a region whose lattice-point count equals N₊ − N₋.

title: Adversarial factorisation game: the only link between levels is CRT consistency
connection: Model: an adversary assigns factorisations to the integers 4Cp+1 (all C) consistently with every congruence p satisfies. ES is the claim that no consistent assignment avoids all certificates. Barrier theorems in the repo are exactly 'consistent avoiding assignments exist for the abstract model'.
why: It locates precisely what a proof must use beyond CRT consistency: the actual multiplicative structure (that the integers really are 4Cp + 1 for one p).
first_step: Write down the minimal 'consistency axioms' satisfied by real factorisations (e.g. gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | 4(C−C′)… and the sizes) that the abstract model violates; any such axiom is a candidate proof ingredient.

title: Gcd structure across levels: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | 4(C′−C)·… as a coupling axiom
connection: For two levels, gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) divides C′(4Cp+1) − C(4C′p+1) = C′ − C. So prime factors are shared between levels only through C′ − C. This is the exact coupling of the family {4Cp+1}.
why: This 'gcd-coupling' is the arithmetic analogue of the dependency graph in LLL/Janson. Any pointwise argument across levels must exploit it.
first_step: Build the level-dependency hypergraph for p via shared primes q | C′ − C, and test whether failure patterns in data are explained by it.

title: OEIS / experimental-math lookup of ES-derived sequences
connection: Sequences such as λ(p), least certificate level, N₋(p), I3_𝒞 least u, the U(n) failure list and the ES₅ failure list. Lookups in OEIS and the Inverse Symbolic Calculator may connect them to unrelated known sequences.
why: It is cheap, native to experimental mathematics, and occasionally finds hidden identities (e.g. a match with a class-number sequence).
first_step: Compute the first 50 terms of 6 derived sequences and search OEIS; record hits.

title: Modular Egyptian fractions: Σ 1/x_i ≡ a (mod q) with small x_i (Erdős–Graham, Shparlinski)
