connection: Erdős–Graham asked which residues mod q are sums of reciprocals of small integers; Shparlinski and others gave results with few terms in short ranges. ES certificates satisfy congruence versions mod 4C, mod d, etc.
why: The modular question is the 'local' shadow of ES; nearest proved results quantify how few small reciprocals cover F_q. It calibrates the local-to-global gap.
first_step: Look up Shparlinski's results on 'sums of reciprocals in residue rings' and their term count/size; formulate the ES-implied congruences and check which are automatically satisfiable.
refs: Shparlinski, On a question of Erdős and Graham (check)

title: Hurwitz quaternions and metacommutation: ES certificates as factorisation patterns
connection: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternion factorisations of a norm-N element are unique up to metacommutation (Conway–Smith; Cohn–Kumar studied the metacommutation permutation). Certificates involve factorisations of p-tied norms in quaternion orders (QUATERNION_ES).
why: Metacommutation is a canonical permutation on factorisations with computable sign/cycle structure. The ES sign might be a metacommutation invariant.
first_step: For small p, compute the factorisations relevant to QUATERNION_ES Type I data in the Hurwitz order and the metacommutation permutation's sign.
refs: Cohn–Kumar, Metacommutation of Hurwitz primes (Proc. AMS 2015)

title: ES over imaginary quadratic rings (e.g. ℤ[i]) as an intermediate test bed
connection: Ask 4/π = 1/ξ + 1/η + 1/ζ over ℤ[i] with a positivity replacement (e.g. ξ,η,ζ in a cone or with positive norm-type constraint). Gaussian primes ≡ 1 mod (2+2i)-type classes play the hard role.
why: There is unique factorisation, and Hecke characters give finer equidistribution. A T1-like obstruction should exist at squares. It is a sibling that tests which ingredients are specific to ℤ.
first_step: Check the literature for 'Erdős–Straus in number fields' (search); define the natural positivity, then compute the analogue of the Mordell hard classes mod small Gaussian moduli.

title: Torus-equivariant localisation: counting words as fixed points of a T-action on a toric variety
connection: Lattice points in a polytope count T-fixed points / sections of line bundles (Brion, Lawrence–Varchenko). Words at fixed t are lattice points on a hyperbola, not a polytope, but at fixed (t,u) the v-condition is linear: the union over (t,u) is a union of 1-dim lattice point sets in progressions.
why: Equivariant localisation gives exact counts with signs (via Brion's formula) and might give a closed form for weighted word counts.
first_step: Write Σ_{words} x^t y^u z^v as a sum of rational generating functions (Brion-type) for each (t,u) cone; examine the analytic structure of the full sum.

title: Barvinok short generating functions for ES certificates up to height B
connection: Barvinok's algorithm encodes lattice points of rational polyhedra as short rational generating functions. ES certificates at fixed level C are lattice points in a union of polyhedra intersected with a hyperbola, which needs a polyhedral approximation.
why: Short generating functions allow evaluation of counts mod 2, character-weighted sums, etc., quickly. This is a computational-native route to exact sign sums.
first_step: Approximate the region by polyhedra (dyadic pieces), compute the Barvinok representation (LattE), and test evaluating weighted sign sums for p ~ 10⁶.

title: Gaussian periods / cyclotomic: (A/p) via the quadratic Gauss sum and certificates as cyclotomic units
connection: (A/p) = σ_A(√p*)/√p* in Q(ζ_p). Words give A with AA* = tp + 1, i.e. A·A* ≡ 1 (mod p), so σ_A σ_{A*} = id. The ES sign is the action of σ_A on the quadratic subfield.
why: Galois-theoretic language: ES₅ ⇔ some word's Galois element σ_A ∈ Gal(Q(ζ_p)/Q) is non-trivial on Q(√p). This connects to Galois-module structure of cyclotomic units (Sinnott) if words relate to units.
first_step: Look for a cyclotomic unit or Gauss-sum expression naturally indexed by words (e.g. (1 − ζ^A)/(1 − ζ)) whose norm to Q(√p) is sign-sensitive.

title: Real quadratic order of γ_w: words as reduced cycles and the sign as a genus/narrow-class invariant
connection: γ_w ∈ SL₂(ℤ) hyperbolic determines a real quadratic order of discriminant (tr γ_w)² − 4 and an ideal class (Latimer–MacDuffee). The ES sign might be a genus character of that class evaluated at p.
why: Latimer–MacDuffee is an exact bijection between conjugacy classes of matrices and ideal classes. The sign then becomes a class-group statement in a family of real quadratic fields.
first_step: Compute the ideal class for γ_w (p < 300) and evaluate genus characters; check whether one equals (A/p).

title: Integer matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial: ES words as conjugacy classes
connection: Words correspond to γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with b = p and a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c). Counting SL₂(ℤ) matrices with given trace and a fixed entry is a classical problem (Eskin–McMullen counting in affine symmetric varieties).
why: Eskin–McMullen/Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak give asymptotic counts in growing balls, which shows the shape of the main term but with no fixed-p pointwise content (B3).
first_step: Note calibration; compute the count of γ with b = p and trace ≤ T as T grows, and its sign-weighted version.
refs: Eskin–McMullen, Mixing, counting, and equidistribution in Lie groups (Duke 1993)

title: Lattice-point counting in −Γ₁(c) with fixed upper-right entry p (Kloosterman/Kuznetsov for Γ₁(c))
connection: ES₅ ⇔ ∃ c ≥ 2, γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), a, d in the word range, and (a/p) = −1. So γ ∈ −Γ₁(c)·(unipotent) with fixed b = p. Kuznetsov's formula for Γ₁(c) (with nebentypus) counts such matrices with smooth weights.
why: It gives the precise spectral-theory native form, with the Jacobi twist making it a metaplectic Kuznetsov (Proskurin) problem. B3 says the main term is too small, but the c-sum gives many groups.
first_step: Write the c-summed count as a sum over Γ₁(c) Kloosterman sums S(0, p; c)-type and record the main term size; check with METAPLECTIC_ES.

title: Integral points on the 'word variety' as an affine homogeneous space under a unipotent group
connection: {γ ∈ SL₂ : b = p} is a homogeneous space for the action of pairs of upper unipotents (left/right translations shift a, d by multiples of p). Words are the integral points with level-structure congruences in a bounded region.
why: Homogeneous-space integral points with congruence conditions are governed by strong approximation (here for a unipotent group, which is trivial) and by the box. This explains why only the archimedean box matters.
first_step: Record: strong approximation for the unipotent group is automatic, so all ES₅ content is in the archimedean box (positivity, sizes). Use as a calibration item for future 'group-action' proposals.

title: Geodesic-flow coding (Series) of γ_w: ES₅ as a closed geodesic with 3 cusp excursions of prescribed depths
connection: Caroline Series' coding links the cutting sequence of a geodesic to its CF expansion, so cusp-excursion depths correspond to partial quotients. A word gives a closed geodesic whose (HJ) coding has 3 blocks of depths (v, t, u), plus a p-condition.
why: Shrinking-target and logarithm-law results (Sullivan) describe cusp excursions statistically. Prescribed exact-depth triples relate to 'periodic orbits with prescribed excursions' counts (Pollicott, Lalley).
first_step: Count closed geodesics whose coding is exactly a 3-block HJ word with depths in given ranges; compare with the word count via the p-constraint.
refs: Series, The modular surface and continued fractions (J. LMS 1985)

title: Fourier–Dedekind sums / Beck–Robins: lattice points in the word region via Dedekind–Rademacher sums
connection: Counting lattice points in rational polytopes yields Fourier–Dedekind sums (Beck–Robins). The ES₅ sign involves Dedekind sums (DEDEKIND_ES). Combining the two might express Σ_{words} (sign) as a finite combination of Dedekind–Rademacher sums.
why: Dedekind–Rademacher sums satisfy reciprocity laws that allow fast evaluation and sometimes positivity statements.
first_step: Express |L₃(p)| and Σ (A/p) for p < 1000 in terms of Dedekind–Rademacher sums r_n(a,b;c) by linear fitting; look for exact identities.

title: Ehrhart theory for the word region: quasi-polynomial in p for fixed letters
connection: For a fixed letter t, the number of words of level t as a function of p is a divisor-type count, not a quasi-polynomial. Restricted to fixed (t,u), it is a periodic function of p (Ehrhart in 1D).
why: It explains exactly where the Ehrhart (polynomial) structure breaks: at the hyperbola. Native calibration.
first_step: Calibration only: write the counts and note the hyperbolic break.

title: Maynard–Tao: infinitely many primes p with many simultaneously prime 4Cp+1 (forced level failures)
connection: If 4Cp + 1 is prime, its only divisors are 1 and itself (≡ 1 mod 4C), so level C fails. Maynard–Tao gives, for admissible tuples of linear forms, infinitely many n with ≥ m of them prime. With n restricted to primes (Maynard's 'dense clusters' framework), this gives infinitely many primes p with ≥ m failed levels among C ≤ K.
why: It would be a PROVED statement about ES-hardness: arbitrarily many small levels fail infinitely often. It calibrates any proof that uses a bounded set of small levels, as a quantitative B1.
first_step: Check whether Maynard's 'Dense clusters of primes in subsets' (Compos. Math. 2016) applies with n ranging over primes and forms 4Cn + 1; state the resulting m(K).
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes (Ann. Math. 2015)
Maynard, Dense clusters of primes in subsets (Compos. Math. 2016)

title: Smooth values of 4Cp+1: certificate abundance when some level is smooth
connection: If 4Cp + 1 is y-smooth with many prime factors, its divisors cover (ℤ/4C)^× (subset products), so a certificate exists. ES would follow from 'for every p some C ≤ (log p)^A has 4Cp + 1 with ≥ k prime factors in general position'.
why: Smooth-number theory (Canfield–Erdős–Pomerance; smooth values of linear forms, Harman; Balog–Wooley) gives existence of smooth values in short families. One value with many factors is a pointwise target with a native toolbox.
first_step: Find the best known result on 'some n ≤ N^ε in a linear family an + b has a smooth or many-factor value' (Balog, Harman), and compare the family length (log p)^A with what is needed.
refs: Granville, Smooth numbers: computational number theory and beyond (2008)

title: Cox 'primes of the form x² + ny²': certificate at level d as a ring-class-field splitting condition
connection: A Type I/II certificate at level d is equivalent to p having a specific representation or splitting behaviour in a ring class field of an order in Q(√−d) (QUATERNION_ES / LATTICE_MEETING). Cox's book gives the exact class-field criterion for such representations.
why: It turns 'certificate at level d' into 'Frobenius of p lies in a set S_d of a Galois group'. ES ⇔ p's Frobenius lies in ∪_d S_d, an infinite union of Chebotarev conditions (the B2 shape).
first_step: For d ≤ 10, write S_d explicitly (ring class field of the relevant conductor) and compute the density covered; compare with the Mordell residue-class picture.
refs: Cox, Primes of the Form x² + ny² (1989)

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli: Type I as p | N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂))
connection: Gross–Zagier: p divides N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂)) iff the two CM orders embed simultaneously into a maximal order of B_{p,∞} (with an explicit formula). QUATERNION_ES shows Type I(p) ⇔ an 'x = 2 collision' of CM orders in B_{p,∞}.
why: It may give a closed criterion: ES Type I at p ⇔ p divides a specific singular-moduli difference. The Gross–Zagier formula expresses the exponent as a sum over representations of binary forms.
first_step: Check numerically for p < 500 whether Type I certificate existence at level d matches p | N(j(√−d)·…) for the orders appearing in Λ_{d,m}.

title: Li–Zhang's proof of Kudla–Rapoport: unitary special cycles and an arithmetic Diff-parity
connection: KUDLA_ES links T1 to oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). In the unitary setting, Li–Zhang proved the Kudla–Rapoport conjecture (arithmetic intersection numbers = derivatives of local densities).
why: If ES certificates are special cycles on a unitary Shimura variety, intersection numbers have exact local formulas, and positivity is geometric.
first_step: Check whether the ES local densities (BM factors) match the local densities in KR for some hermitian lattice of rank 2 or 3 over Q(√−p) or Q(i).
refs: Li–Zhang, On the arithmetic Siegel–Weil formula for GSpin Shimura varieties / Kudla–Rapoport (Invent. 2022; check)

title: V_n as values of the indefinite binary form nA² − 2μAB + B² on its Conway topograph
connection: V_n: nA² + B² + D = 2μAB means the form Q(A,B) = nA² − 2μAB + B² takes the value −D with D | μ. On Conway's topograph of Q (disc 4(μ² − n) = 4f), the values along the river are periodic, and ES points are river-adjacent values −D with D | μ at (A even, B = 1).
why: Topograph navigation gives all small values of an indefinite form exactly. ES becomes: for some μ, the river of Q_μ shows a value −D with D | μ at a B = 1 position.
first_step: For n = p < 500 and μ ≤ 3√p, draw/compute river values of Q_μ and mark ES points; look for a pattern in where they occur along the period.

title: Continued fraction of √f, f = μ² − n: Lagrange's |value| < 2√f and V_n points among convergents
connection: Small values of an indefinite binary form occur at convergents of its roots (Lagrange: |Q(A,B)| < 2√f/… ⇒ (B,A) is a convergent-type pair). V_n points with small D are therefore convergents of (μ ± √f)/n.
why: This makes V_n points a CF computation, with period-length and Pell-unit structure, and connects to ES's other CF forms (HJ length).
first_step: Verify that every V_n point at μ with D < √f comes from a convergent of (μ + √f)/n; then express the B = 1 condition as a condition on the convergent index.

title: Unexplained empty fibre S_{3861,4}(ℕ) = ∅: non-BM obstruction (Harpaz-type) or a second Brauer class?
connection: Z52 records unexplained zeros of the pencil fibres S_{n,k}(ℕ), e.g. S_{3861,4} with n ≡ 5 (mod 8). Harpaz shows that on some log K3 surfaces BM is not the only obstruction to integral points.
why: An explained zero would either give a new Brauer class (a new obstruction mechanism near ES) or the first example of a non-BM obstruction in the ES pencil. Both sharpen the map near k = 0.
first_step: Compute Br(S_{3861,4})/Br(ℚ) (algebraic part via the toric/conic structure) and evaluate all classes on local points; if all evaluations allow points, check the archimedean/positivity piece separately.

title: Pencil fibres with non-square k: does any Brauer class survive, and what are the zero statistics?
connection: The Z52 theorem covers k = m². For non-square k, Br S_{n,k} may differ, and the k = 0 limit is approached through both square and non-square k. Data on zeros of S_{n,k} for non-square k is the natural sibling table.
why: If non-square fibres have no obstruction and no zeros, the k = 0 fibre's behaviour is 'squares-only obstructed', mirroring T1 in the k-direction.
first_step: Tabulate S_{n,k}(ℕ) = ∅ for n < 10⁴, k ∈ {2, 3, 5, 6, 7}; compare with BM predictions computed from the conic-bundle structure.

title: Semigroup orbit counting (Bourgain–Kontorovich, Kontorovich–Oh) for the ES word semigroup with entry p
connection: QUESTION_R casts words as elements of a semigroup Ψ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ)_{≥0}. Thin-orbit counting with congruence conditions gives asymptotic counts of orbit elements with entry ≤ N in progressions (level of distribution).
why: This gives averaged ES₅ results with power savings, and RS's local–global theorem shows that for fat semigroups the sporadic set is finite. The ES semigroup's exponent δ decides which regime applies.
first_step: Compute the critical exponent δ of the semigroup generated by the word letters (likely 1, i.e. not thin). If δ = 1, record that RS-type local–global for 'fat' semigroups is the relevant theorem class.

title: Heilbronn's average CF length with a quadratic-character twist
connection: Heilbronn: the average number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm on a/p is (12 log 2/π²) log p. Twisting by (a/p), the difference between average lengths over QR and QNR a is a 'character-correlated CF statistic'.
why: If QNRs have systematically shorter/longer expansions (in HJ form), that is a global bias relevant to λ(p) ≤ 3. Twisted Heilbronn sums reduce to Kloosterman-type sums (Ustinov's methods).
first_step: Compute mean HJ length over QR vs QNR a for p < 10⁵; test whether the difference is O(1) or decays.
refs: Ustinov, on statistical properties of finite continued fractions (check)

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo: rank-1 lattice rules with generator A and HJ length 3 as 'worst' lattices
connection: A 2-D rank-1 lattice rule {(k/p, kA/p)} has quality governed by the partial quotients of A/p (Zaremba index; Niederreiter). HJ length 3 with huge digits means a very bad lattice rule. ES₅ asks for a bad lattice rule with a QNR generator.
why: QMC has existence theorems for good lattice rules for all p (Korobov) and explicit constructions for prime powers (Niederreiter). The extremal-bad side with a character condition is a dual question.
first_step: Formulate ES₅ in QMC terms: ∃ QNR A such that the lattice rule has a lattice point (v, u) with uv small and vA − u = p (the dual lattice has a very short vector). Compare with Korobov averaging over A ∈ QNR.
refs: Niederreiter, Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods (1992)

title: Minkowski question-mark function: ?(A/p) as a dyadic rational with prescribed run structure
connection: ?(x) maps the CF of x to a binary expansion with run lengths equal to the partial quotients. ES₅ asks for a QNR A whose ?(A/p) (or an HJ analogue) has a 3-block structure.
why: It gives a singular-measure (Minkowski measure) viewpoint: the set of A/p with short expansions is where ?-measure concentrates on few dyadic blocks. It is close to the Stern item but uses measure-theoretic tools.
first_step: Compute ?(A/p) for A ∈ L₃(p) and look for structure (e.g. ? values lie in a few dyadic intervals); compare QR vs QNR.

title: Configuration-model random graph for F_p with the divisor-degree sequence
connection: Model F_p as a random graph with the same degree sequence (degrees = numbers of valid partners). Component-size predictions (Molloy–Reed criterion) show whether the component of 1 should be giant.
why: It gives a quantitative null model for forest connectivity, and deviations would show the arithmetic is non-random in a usable way.
first_step: Compute the degree sequence of F_p and the Molloy–Reed quantity Σ d(d−2); compare predicted and actual component sizes for p < 10⁶.

title: Pretentious multiplicative functions: forest monochromaticity forces χ_p to 'pretend' to be 1
connection: If ES₅ fails, χ_p(u) = χ_p(v) on all forest edges (forest form). For a completely multiplicative ±1 function this is a strong constraint along a sparse set of multiplicative relations. Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness quantifies when f behaves like 1 on structured sets.
why: Halász-type theorems give strong conclusions from pretentiousness. If edge constraints imply Σ_{q ≤ X}(1 − χ_p(q))/q small, this would contradict known lower bounds for the least QNR's 'pretentious distance' (or not).
first_step: Translate the edge constraints χ(u)χ(v) = 1 into constraints on χ at primes for small u, v; compute the implied D(χ_p, 1; X) bound and compare with Burgess-type lower bounds.
refs: Granville–Soundararajan, Pretentious multiplicative functions and an inequality for the zeta-function (2008)

title: Borel–Cantelli heuristic: Σ_p P(no certificate at p) < ∞ under various independence models
connection: With P(fail at p) ≈ exp(−c log²p) the sum converges, so heuristically only finitely many failures exist and they would be small (all excluded below 10¹⁸). This is the probabilistic native statement of 'ES is true'.
why: Calibration: makes precise which correlation model must hold for the heuristic, and how much heavier the lower tail would have to be to allow infinitely many failures (log P(0) ≥ −log p).
first_step: From repo LDP data, fit log P(0|M) and compute the threshold tail behaviour that would make Σ_p diverge; compare with Markoff (Ghosh–Sarnak) where infinitely many failures occur.

title: Elsholtz-style generalised windmills for x² + ny² as templates for ES windmills
connection: Zagier's one-sentence proof generalises (Elsholtz; Jackson et al.) to involution proofs that primes in certain classes are represented by x² + 2y², x² + 3y², etc. These are verified parity proofs for 'one representation exists' at primes in classes.
why: These are the closest proved windmill-type pointwise theorems. Their combinatorial skeleton (sets of triples with linear involutions) is the template that WINDMILL/INVOLUTION_ES look for, so the known catalogue tells what forms are reachable.
first_step: Collect the known windmill proofs (x² + ny², n ∈ {1,2,3,…}) and their set definitions; check whether the ES Type II data (4abd = pe + 1) can be fitted to any of their shapes.
refs: Elsholtz, A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems (2010; check)

title: Characteristic-p degeneracies of function-field ES (4 = 0 in char 2, 4 = 1 in char 3)
connection: Over F_{2^k}[T], 4/P = 0, so ES asks for three unit fractions summing to 0, which is P-independent and solvable (e.g. 1/T + 1/(T+1) + 1/(T(T+1)) = 0). Over F_{3^k}[T], 4/P = 1/P. These degenerations separate the role of the numerator 4 from the denominator's arithmetic.
why: Cheap sanity variants that test which function-field proofs use the size or arithmetic of the numerator 4 (and the 2-adic slot structure).
first_step: Work out ES over F_{3^k}[T]: is 1/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with monic X, Y, Z always solvable, and by what identity?

title: Ibukiyama's explicit maximal orders O(q,r) in B_{p,∞} vs the ES orders Λ_{d,m}
connection: Ibukiyama gives explicit maximal orders of B_{p,∞} in terms of q ≡ 3 mod 8 with (−q/p) = −1 and r² ≡ −p mod q. ES's Λ_{d,m} are orders in definite algebras defined by u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1. Embedding Λ_{d,m} into O(q,r) links certificates to the choice of auxiliary prime q.
why: Ibukiyama orders are the standard computational model. The auxiliary-prime choice resembles ES's least-QNR dependence (q with (−q/p) = −1).
first_step: For p < 200, test which Λ_{d,m} embed into Ibukiyama orders with small q and compare with certificate levels.
refs: Ibukiyama, On maximal orders of division quaternion algebras over the rational number field with certain optimal embeddings (Nagoya 1982)

title: ES₅ for p ≡ 5 (8) vs p ≡ 1 (8): different native fields for the two classes
connection: The five-slice equivalence λ(p) ≤ 3 is stated for p ≡ 1 (8). For p ≡ 5 (8), (2/p) = −1 gives cheap certificates. In lattice/sandpile terms, p mod 8 is the Gauss-sum class (Brown invariant) of the discriminant form, so different topological constraints apply.
why: Splitting by p mod 8 is natural in every field (Arf invariant of knots with det p, Brown invariant of linking forms). The hard class p ≡ 1 (8) is where the Arf invariant of a det-p knot is 0.
first_step: Record the per-class status (which classes are trivial, by which certificate) and check whether p ≡ 1 (8) hard primes correspond to knots with Arf = 0 and signature ≡ 0 (mod 8).

title: Eisenstein–Kronecker / Lerch: word counts as special values of partial zeta functions
connection: Sums over divisors in residue classes are partial zeta values of ℚ at s = 0 for ray classes. Per-p word counts are finite combinations of such divisor sums, possibly expressible via partial zeta values of real quadratic fields (via γ_w).
why: Partial zeta values at s = 0 are rational and given by Shintani/Siegel formulas, which could turn the sign sum into a finite computable rational expression with integrality.
first_step: Attempt: express Σ_{words} (A/p) at prime p as Σ of ζ(0, 𝔞) over narrow ideal classes of Q(√D) for D from traces; check numerically for small p.
refs: Shintani 1976 (values of zeta at non-positive integers)

title: Gauss composition of the word forms: is there a group law on words of fixed level t?
connection: Words of level t correspond to factorisations N_t = A·A* with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t), i.e. to ideal-like objects. If they correspond to ideals in an order (e.g. of disc −4t or t² − 4), composition may combine words of p₁ and p₂ into words of p₁p₂-related N.
why: A composition law gives a multiplicative structure on certificates, the missing 'algebraic rigidity' (R-type) in FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Test: given words of level t at n₁ and n₂, is there a natural word of level t at some n₃ = f(n₁,n₂) (e.g. via (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t·n₃ + 1 with n₃ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂)? Check sign multiplicativity.

title: The multiplicative monoid (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t(tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂) + 1: ES₅ transport n₁ ⋆_t n₂
connection: The set {N : N ≡ 1 (mod t)} is a multiplicative monoid, and n ↦ tn + 1 transports the operation n₁ ⋆ n₂ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂. Words of level t at n₁ and n₂ give factorisations whose products are factorisations of N(n₁ ⋆ n₂) with factors ≡ 1 (mod t), not −1. Mixing parities yields −1 classes.
why: It is an explicit transport law candidate: ES₅ data at n₁, n₂ might produce data at n₁ ⋆_t n₂. Iterated, the failure set must be closed under the inverse operation.
first_step: Compute: from words (A₁, A₁*) at n₁ and (A₂, A₂*) at n₂, does A₁A₂* (≡ +1 mod t) or A₁·(something) give a valid word at n₁ ⋆ n₂? Check by brute force for small n.

title: Lens space surgery obstruction: QNR lens spaces are exactly those not obtainable by integral surgery on a knot (homotopy class)
connection: p-surgery on a knot K ⊂ S³ gives H₁ = ℤ/p with linking form ±1/p, so a lens space L(p,q) arising this way has ±q a square mod p. For p ≡ 1 (4) that means (q/p) = +1. Hence ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space that is homotopically not an integral knot surgery bounds a 3-chain plumbing. Greene's solution of the lens space realisation problem uses exactly plumbing-lattice embeddings.
why: It locates the ES sign in a famous problem: Greene's lattice-embedding classification (via changemaker lattices) gives a complete description of the square class side. The ES side is its complement.
first_step: Read Greene (Ann. Math. 2013), §§1–3. Check whether the changemaker-lattice machinery has a version for the non-square linking class (e.g. surgeries on knots in other 3-manifolds) that yields 3-chain plumbings.
refs: Greene, The lens space realization problem (Ann. Math. 2013)

title: Honda's count of tight contact structures on L(p,A): (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p/A = [[v,t,u]]
connection: Honda: the number of tight contact structures on L(p,q) up to isotopy is ∏(b_i − 1) over the HJ digits of p/q. So ES₅ words are lens spaces of order p with exactly three-factor tight counts in the non-square homotopy class, and I3 (letters ≥ 3) means every factor is ≥ 2.
why: Contact topology adds a natural weight (the tight-structure count) to each word. Weighted counts Σ_A ∏(b_i − 1)(A/p) might be more regular than plain counts (e.g. given by a Heegaard Floer formula).
first_step: Compute the weighted sum W±(p) = Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p), (A/p)=±1} (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p < 10⁵ and look for a closed form.
refs: Honda, On the classification of tight contact structures I (Geom. Topol. 2000)

title: Cohen–Lenstra for sandpile groups (Wood) and the distribution of pairing classes on random graphs
connection: Wood proved sandpile groups of random graphs follow a Cohen–Lenstra-type law, including the pairing (Clancy–Kaplan–Leake–Payne–Wood conjectures; Wood's 'random graphs' theorem). For graphs with cyclic group ℤ/p, the pairing class is ±square with predictable probabilities.
why: It gives a theorem-level random model for ES₅'s sign: 'random small graphs with τ = p have a non-square pairing with probability ≈ 1/2'. ES₅ is a fixed-shape (fan) specialisation.
first_step: Read Wood, The distribution of sandpile groups of random graphs (JAMS 2017); compute the empirical pairing-class frequency over all fan words for p < 10⁵ vs the CL prediction.
refs: Wood, The distribution of sandpile groups of random graphs (JAMS 2017)
Clancy–Kaplan–Leake–Payne–Wood, On a Cohen–Lenstra heuristic for Jacobians of random graphs (J. Algebraic Combin. 2015)

title: K₄-multigraph rung: any 4-vertex multigraph with τ = p and non-square pairing
connection: Relax the fan shape to an arbitrary multigraph on 4 vertices (six edge multiplicities). Its τ is the Kirchhoff polynomial of K₄ in the multiplicities, and the pairing is read from the reduced Laplacian. This 6-parameter problem contains ES₅ (fan) as a 3-parameter slice.
why: It is the natural intermediate rung between ES₅ and 'any graph'. Its failure set might be empty for all p > small, which would locate exactly what the fan shape costs.
first_step: Enumerate 4-vertex multigraphs with τ = p, p < 2·10⁴, record non-square pairing existence; list failures.

title: The L-ladder in cluster language: λ(p) ≤ L ⇔ an (L+2)-gon frieze with one coefficient side N = p and a mod-4 entry
connection: Words of HJ length L are friezes of the (L+2)-gon with all boundary sides 1 except one side N. CHJ prove finiteness for given boundary. The slot lemma presumably generalises (via van der Blij) to 'some diagonal ≡ 0 mod 4'.
why: It gives a uniform family of cluster-algebraic statements (types A_{L−1} with coefficient). L = 3 is ES₅, and λ(p) ≤ L for growing L is Zaremba-adjacent and provable.
first_step: Verify the generalised slot lemma for L = 4 numerically (sign of A vs 4-divisibility of frieze diagonals) for p < 10⁴.

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD-graph compression for the dependency structure across levels
connection: The Duffin–Schaeffer proof controls sets of integers with many pairs of large gcd by iterative 'GCD graph' compression. ES levels C are coupled through gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | C′ − C. A GCD-graph style structure theorem might show that simultaneous failure of many levels forces a structured (compressible) configuration.
why: It is a modern combinatorial-analytic technique for exactly the 'many dependent arithmetic events' situation, and it has not obviously been tried.
first_step: Read Koukoulopoulos–Maynard (Ann. Math. 2020) §§5–7; formulate the ES level-failure configuration as a weighted graph on levels with edge weights from shared primes.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture (Ann. Math. 2020)

title: Toric log del Pezzo / weighted projective planes from Egyptian triples (Nill–Kasprzyk dictionary)
connection: Unit-fraction equations classify reflexive/Gorenstein toric Fano simplices (1 = Σ 1/k_i ↔ weighted projective spaces P(q₀,…) with q_i | Σq). For ES, the weights (yz, xz, xy)/g give a weighted P² whose 'index' (Σq)/lcm(q) is tied to 4/n. ES ⇔ some weighted P² has a prescribed index-type invariant.
why: The toric-Fano classification literature (Kasprzyk, Nill, Conrads) has tools for exactly 'which weight vectors satisfy divisibility conditions'. That gives a geometric home for the original Egyptian equation.
first_step: Work out the exact invariant: for P(a,b,c) with (a,b,c) ∝ (1/x,1/y,1/z), compute (a+b+c)/lcm(a,b,c) and the Gorenstein index in terms of n; check against Kasprzyk's tables of fake weighted planes.
refs: Conrads, Weighted projective spaces and reflexive simplices (2002)
Kasprzyk, Bounds on fake weighted projective space (2009; check)

title: Matrix relaxation: 4/n = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for integer positive definite M in a class (diagonal = ES)
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 1ᵀ diag(x,y,z)⁻¹ 1. Replacing diagonal matrices by tridiagonal chain matrices gives 1ᵀM⁻¹1 = (tu + tv + uv + 2u + 2v)/(tuv − u − v). The problem 'every 4/n is 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for M in a class 𝒞' interpolates between ES and lattice problems.
why: For rich classes 𝒞 (all positive definite integer M) it is trivially solvable; for diagonal it is ES. The threshold class is a measure of how special the diagonal (Egyptian) structure is. 1ᵀM⁻¹1 is an effective conductance.
first_step: Test 𝒞 = {diagonal + one off-diagonal −1}: is every 4/p = 1ᵀM⁻¹1 for such M? Compute for p < 10⁴.

title: Schreier graph of SL₂(ℤ) on P¹(F_p) (Selberg's 3/16): HJ length as a path length with unbounded generators
connection: The HJ step A ↦ ⌈p/A⌉A − p is a move on P¹(F_p)-type data, and r(p/A) is a path length from A to 0 in a graph with generators M(b) for all b. The bounded-generator Schreier graph is an expander (Selberg's eigenvalue bound).
why: It explains (B3) why expansion does not give length-3 paths: unbounded generators collapse the diameter, and existence of length-3 paths into a coset is not spectral. It is recorded as the native picture.
first_step: Compute, in the bounded-generator Schreier graph (b ≤ B), the distance from ∞ to the QNR set as a function of B and p; compare with λ(p).

title: Quadratic large sieve over p for the families S₃(p): exceptional-set bounds
connection: The large sieve for real characters (Heath-Brown) bounds Σ_p |Σ_{n} a_n (n/p)|². ES₅ failure at p needs (A/p) = 1 on S₃(p), but S₃ varies with p. EXCEPTIONAL_LARGESIEVE pursues this.
why: It is the native tool for exceptional sets; recorded to complete the map.
first_step: See EXCEPTIONAL_LARGESIEVE*.md for the current exponent; no new action here.

title: Integer-relation search (PSLQ/LLL) for N₋(p) or the slot-count in a basis of arithmetic functions
connection: Try to express N₋(p), N₊(p) or the ES₅ word count as an integer combination of standard arithmetic functions of p and p-tied integers (τ(p+k), class numbers h(−kp), r₂, r₃(kp), …).
why: A found identity is a candidate exact formula (an R-type rigidity). A null result over a large basis is evidence against simple formulas. SIGN_IDENTITY did a version; the basis can be widened.
first_step: Build a basis of 200 functions evaluated at 2000 primes; run integer relation detection (LLL on the evaluation matrix) for N₋(p).

title: Explicit Burgess (Treviño) to make the 'BM layer is pointwise free' statement fully explicit
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 Prop 2.2: some 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive BM main term iff p is not a square. Explicit Burgess bounds (Treviño, McGown) give explicit ℓ(p) ≤ p^{1/4√e+ε}-type bounds with constants.
why: It gives an explicit, verifiable statement that is the first layer of ES, for formal verification and for any explicit-range argument.
first_step: Plug Treviño's explicit least-QNR bound into Prop 2.2; state the explicit level bound for all p ≥ 10²⁰.
refs: Treviño, The least quadratic non-residue and related problems (2015; check)

title: Rare-event simulation (importance sampling / multilevel splitting) for P(no certificate)
connection: Direct sampling sees zeros only at small M (mean count). Rare-event methods from statistical physics (cloning, splitting, importance sampling under a tilted factorisation model) estimate P(N = 0 | M) far into the tail.
why: It tests the large-deviation heuristic (exponent vs M) in a regime unreachable by enumeration, which matters for the Borel–Cantelli calibration.
first_step: Implement a tilted Kubilius-model sampler for factorisations of 4Cp+1 across levels; estimate log P(0) for M up to 40.

title: Persistent homology of the certificate point cloud as p varies
connection: Represent the certificates of p as points (e.g. (log t, log u, log v) for words) and compute persistent homology across p. Topological features (holes) that persist might indicate excluded regions such as T1-like voids.
why: This is a TDA-native exploratory lens. It may flag structure (voids) not visible in counts. Low prior.
first_step: Compute Vietoris–Rips persistence for the word clouds of 100 primes near 10⁶ vs 100 near-squares; compare barcodes.

title: Siegel-zero world: does an exceptional character help ES (Heath-Brown twin-prime-style)?
connection: Heath-Brown showed that a Siegel zero would imply twin primes. In a Siegel-zero world, one real character χ_D pretends to be μ-like, which strongly biases factorisations of integers in progressions. ES's level classes involve χ_{−t}, so a Siegel zero for some −t might force divisor classes.
why: Conditional on a Siegel zero, extreme bias sometimes proves pointwise statements. Conditional on its absence, standard tools apply. A dichotomy proof (either case gives ES) is a known proof pattern.
first_step: Work out how an exceptional χ_{−t₀} affects the distribution of divisor classes of tp+1 mod t₀; check whether it forces −1 classes.
refs: Heath-Brown, Prime twins and Siegel zeros (Proc. LMS 1983)

title: Standard-conjecture matrix: GRH, Elliott–Halberstam, Schinzel H, Chowla, Cramér vs ES/ES₅/I3
connection: FRONTIER says no standard conjecture is known to imply I3, ES₅ or ES. A matrix with rows = conjectures and columns = ES variants, recording what each gives (density, exceptional-set rate, pointwise), is the native 'conditional results' table.
why: It locates exactly which non-standard hypothesis is needed (e.g. 'divisors of one integer equidistribute in classes'), a useful formal target.
first_step: Check CONDITIONAL_ES.md; fill in missing cells (e.g. Chowla for (·/p) along words, EH for levels).

title: Effective Chebotarev in the compositum of Q(√−t, ζ_t) over all small t: the joint Frobenius of p
connection: ES certificate existence at levels t ≤ T is a function of p's Frobenius in a large compositum K_T (genus fields, ray class fields) plus the factorisation of tp+1. The first part is Chebotarev; the second is not Galois-theoretic.
why: It cleanly separates the Galois-theoretic layer (handled by Chebotarev/GRH) from the 'factorisation of one integer' layer, which is where B2 lives.
first_step: Define K_T explicitly for T ≤ 12; compute which Frobenius classes guarantee a certificate (from the Galois layer alone) and their density.

title: Pell-like recurrence: words at p from words at smaller primes via SL₂ conjugation by a fixed matrix
connection: Conjugating γ_w by a fixed S ∈ SL₂(ℤ) preserves trace but moves the entry p to a new value b′ = linear in (a,b,c,d). Integer orbits of the conjugation action on {γ with b prime} are Pell-like recurrences relating words of different primes.
why: It gives transport laws with group structure (like Vieta jumping). If a recurrence preserves the sign and sizes, failures would propagate along orbits.
first_step: For S = [[1,1],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[1,1]], compute how words transform (when the image is a word) and how the sign changes.

title: Elkies-style 'search for structure' in large-height ES solutions via lattice reduction
connection: Elkies's ABC/Euler-conjecture searches use lattice reduction to find large solutions with structure. For ES, solutions with exceptionally large minimal x (hardest p) might be found by targeted lattice search, giving data on 'how hard' primes look.
why: It is the computational-NT native way to probe extreme cases, giving better test cases than random primes.
first_step: Search primes p < 10¹⁵ near pseudosquares for the maximal least-certificate level using lattice-guided sampling; record extremes.

title: Egyptian fractions over the p-adics with archimedean positivity: a 'local-global' table per place
connection: For each place v, ES is solvable over ℤ_v (and positively over ℝ). The obstruction is global. An adelic-orbit/Tamagawa view gives the BM main term as ∏_v vol(U_n(ℤ_v)). The 2-adic factor carries the slot-lemma condition.
why: It records the native adelic computation that the repo already uses (BM_CORRECTED_COUNT); here the point is a per-place table of the slot-lemma 2-adic measure.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic measure of the set of words with some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4), as a function of p mod 8.

title: Exact Seifert/pretzel form: ES(n) ⇔ a Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) with Euler number −4/n (double cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z))
connection: The Seifert space over S² with unnormalised invariants (x,1),(y,1),(z,1) has rational Euler number e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = xy + yz + zx. It is the double branched cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z), with det P = xy + yz + zx. So ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel link P(x,y,z) has det = 4xyz/n ⇔ some such Seifert space has e = −4/n.
why: It is an exact translation of the original equation into 3-manifold/knot language. The fields have structure theorems for pretzel knots (sliceness, genus, Heegaard Floer) and for Seifert invariants, with n appearing as the Euler number.
first_step: Tabulate, for n < 200, the pretzel links P(x,y,z) realising ES solutions; check whether Type I/II solution families correspond to natural pretzel families (e.g. one strand dividing another) and whether T1 square classes relate to slice pretzel knots (Greene–Jabuka; det must be a square).
refs: Greene–Jabuka, The slice-ribbon conjecture for 3-stranded pretzel knots (Amer. J. Math. 2011)

title: Montesinos relaxation: Euler number −4/n with arbitrary numerators β_i (M(0; β₁/x, β₂/y, β₃/z))
connection: Allowing Seifert invariants (x,β₁),(y,β₂),(z,β₃) gives β₁/x + β₂/y + β₃/z = 4/n, which is trivially solvable. Requiring all β_i = 1 is ES; requiring β_i ∈ {1, 2} is an intermediate rung.
why: It gives a relaxation ladder native to Seifert/Montesinos knots, where the rung β_i ≤ 2 might be provable and might reveal which numerator constraint carries the difficulty.
first_step: Test 'β_i ∈ {1,2}' (i.e. 4/n = Σ ε_i/x_i with ε_i ∈ {1,2}) for all primes < 10⁷; find whether a uniform construction exists.

title: Quantum modular forms / Ẑ-invariants of the ES Seifert spaces
connection: WRT invariants and GPPV Ẑ-invariants of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres are false-theta functions, i.e. quantum modular forms (Lawrence–Zagier for the Poincaré sphere; Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa). ES Seifert spaces M(0; 1/x,1/y,1/z) with e = −4/n form a family indexed by solutions.
why: Sum over solutions of a quantum invariant gives a generating object attached to n. Speculative, but it puts the solution set into an automorphic-adjacent structure different from Thm K.
first_step: Compute Ẑ (GPPV formula for Seifert spaces) for the ES Seifert spaces of small n and inspect the dependence on n.
refs: Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa, BPS spectra and 3-manifold invariants (2017; check arXiv)
Lawrence–Zagier, Modular forms and quantum invariants of 3-manifolds (1999)

title: Markov uniqueness at prime powers (Baragar, Button, Schmutz) as a pointwise-at-primes precedent
connection: The Markov uniqueness conjecture is proved when the largest Markov number is a prime power (Baragar; Button; Schmutz), using the factorisation/roots of x² ≡ −1 (mod m) and the arithmetic of 9m² − 4. It is a pointwise statement at primes about a Markoff-type equation, proved via the arithmetic of a p-tied integer.
why: It is a rare (R)-type rigidity result at primes for a Markoff-type surface; ES's S_{n,D} is Markoff-type. Its mechanism (counting square roots of −1 mod p) is cheap and might transfer to counting certificate roots mod p.
first_step: Read Button, 'The uniqueness of the prime Markoff numbers' (J. LMS 1998); identify the step where primality is used and check whether an analogous root count constrains S_{p,D} solutions.
refs: Button, The uniqueness of the prime Markoff numbers (J. LMS 1998)
Aigner, Markov's Theorem and 100 Years of the Uniqueness Conjecture (2013)

title: Cohn matrices / Markov-tree calculus for products M(v)M(t)M(u)
connection: Markov numbers are entries of Cohn matrices, i.e. products of two generators along the Markov tree, and Christoffel words index them. ES words are length-3 products in the HJ generators. Cohn's calculus (trace identities, Fricke relations tr(AB) + tr(AB⁻¹) = tr A tr B) gives algebraic relations among such products.
why: Fricke trace identities make the Markoff equation appear from SL₂ traces. A trace-identity derivation of S_{n,D} from words would unify MARKOFF_ES and the HJ forms.
first_step: Compute tr(M(v)M(t)M(u)) and Fricke-related traces of pairs of word matrices; search for the relation nA² + B² + D = ABC among them.

title: SL₂-character variety of the punctured torus / pair of pants: S_{n,D} as a relative character variety
connection: Markoff-type cubics x² + y² + z² − xyz = k are relative SL₂-character varieties of the once-punctured torus (k = boundary trace + 2). The mapping class group acts, and that action drives BGS/Chen. S_{n,D} might be a character variety of a different surface or with a twisted boundary condition, or might not be one at all.
why: If S_{n,D} is a (twisted) character variety, a mapping-class-group action exists, which is exactly the missing infinite group action; if not, that is a structural reason for the difference from Markoff.
first_step: Test whether nA² + B² + D − ABC can be transformed (rescaling, sign changes over ℚ(√n)) into a character-variety cubic x² + y² + z² − xyz − k; compute the invariants (discriminant, singular points) to decide.
refs: Goldman, The modular group action on real SL(2)-characters of a one-holed torus (Geom. Topol. 2003)

title: Temperley bijection: ES₅ fan ↔ a planar bipartite graph with exactly p perfect matchings
connection: Temperley's bijection maps spanning trees of a planar graph G to perfect matchings of a derived bipartite graph. The fan multigraph with τ = p therefore yields a planar bipartite graph with p dimer configurations; Kasteleyn matrices compute them as determinants, and height functions carry signs.
why: Dimer models have height functions and Kasteleyn signs; the ES sign (pairing class) might be a dimer observable, e.g. the parity of height-function flux around a face.
first_step: Construct the Temperley graph of the fan for small words and compute the Kasteleyn matrix; test whether a height-function statistic mod 2 matches the slot-lemma sign.

title: Small levels as norm forms: level-t failure for t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} ⇔ tp+1 is (roughly) a norm from Q(√−t)-type orders
connection: A divisor of tp + 1 that is ≡ −1 (mod t) exists iff some prime factor lies outside the subgroup generated by the classes splitting appropriately. For t = 4 this means 'some prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4)', so level-4 failure ⇔ 4p+1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇔ 4p+1 is a sum of two coprime squares. Similar statements hold for t = 3 (norms from ℤ[ω]).
why: This makes the first levels' failure a Landau–Ramanujan-type 'values of a linear form that are norms' property. Iwaniec's half-dimensional sieve proves that infinitely many p have 4p+1 a sum of two squares, so this gives a PROVED infinite family of level-4 failures.
first_step: Compute the density of p for which all levels t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} fail (simultaneous norm conditions), and the sieve-dimension of that set; compare with data.
refs: Iwaniec, Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A where φ is a quadratic form (Acta Arith. 1972)

title: Unifying lemma across fields: pairing class = slot-lemma sign = lens homotopy class = K-matrix anyon class
connection: For a word (t,u,v), the following should be the same bit: (A/p); the sandpile pairing class of the fan; Whitehead's homotopy class of L(p,A); the discriminant-form class of the chain lattice/K-matrix; the slot-lemma 4-divisibility indicator; the sign of Zolotarev's permutation x ↦ Ax.
why: A single table with proofs makes the ES₅ sign transportable to every listed field, so that a theorem in any of them is immediately an ES₅ statement.
first_step: Write the one-page dictionary with proofs (each equality is short: the discriminant form is A/p in all cases) and check it numerically on all words for p < 10⁴.

title: Meta: the chain matrix M(t,u,v) as a common carrier in ≥ 8 fields — a transfer table of nearest theorems
connection: M(t,u,v) is simultaneously a reduced Laplacian, an electrical network, a ternary Gram matrix, a plumbing intersection form, a cyclic-quotient resolution graph, a FQH K-matrix, an A₂ frieze with coefficient and an SL₂ word. For each field, record the strongest pointwise existence theorem about this object.
why: It organises the translation work so that a single new theorem in one field can be checked for transfer to all others.
first_step: Build the table (field, object, nearest pointwise theorem, what it would need) from items in this lane; mark empty cells as targets.

title: Resistor-network rung: n/4 as the resistance of any 3-resistor integer network
connection: Three integer resistors in parallel give ES. The other 3-resistor topologies (series + parallel mixes: x + (y‖z), (x + y)‖z) give other Diophantine conditions. 'Every n/4 is realised by some 3-resistor network' is a rung that contains ES.
why: Calibration: it shows whether ES's difficulty is specific to the all-parallel topology. A cheap computation decides it for small n.
first_step: For n < 10⁶, check realisability of n/4 by each 3-resistor topology; list the n realisable only via the parallel one and those not realisable at all.

title: Tetrahedral analogue: 1/r = Σ 1/h_i over four faces (four-term Egyptian in 3D)
connection: For a tetrahedron, 1/r = Σ_{i=1}^4 1/h_i (inradius vs altitudes). The triangle identity 1/r = Σ 1/h_i (three terms) is the 2D version behind the altitude form of ES. Higher-dimensional simplices give k-term Egyptian equations with geometric realisability conditions.
why: It places ES in a dimension ladder of simplex geometry, where realisability (simplex inequalities) adds constraints. Low priority, but it is a natural family.
first_step: Record; optionally test whether 4/n = Σ 1/h_i (4 terms) with tetrahedron realisability is always solvable.

title: Pinwheel / periodic scheduling with three unit tasks of density exactly 4/n
connection: In periodic scheduling, three unit-time tasks with periods x, y, z have total density 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. ES ⇔ some such task system has density exactly 4/n. The pinwheel problem studies schedulability of density vectors (Kawamura recently proved the 5/6-density conjecture).
why: Mostly a restatement, but scheduling theory has combinatorial classification tools for unit-fraction density vectors (harmonic periods, folding).
first_step: Check whether pinwheel literature contains structural results about which unit-fraction triples have prescribed sums; otherwise record as restatement only.
refs: Kawamura, Proof of the density threshold conjecture for pinwheel scheduling (STOC 2024; check)

title: Values of rational symmetric functions on ℕ³: e₂/e₃ = 4/n
connection: ES(n) ⇔ the rational symmetric function e₂/e₃ = Σ 1/x_i takes the value 4/n on ℕ³. Value sets of symmetric rational functions on integer points connect to Vieta-type substitutions and to the 'totally split cubic' item.
why: It is a symmetric-function lens. Power-sum/elementary transitions might give alternative parametrisations, e.g. through e₁ (sum) or p₂.
first_step: Write ES in (e₁, e₂, e₃) with 4e₃ = n·e₂ and study integrality of the roots via the discriminant; compute which (e₁, e₂) give totally split cubics for small n.

title: Riemenschneider point diagram: dual chains and the sign under p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: The Riemenschneider dual of p/A is p/(p − A), and (p−A/p) = (A/p) for p ≡ 1 (4). Duality maps length-3 chains (v,t,u) to chains of length v + t + u − 5. So ES₅ is also a statement about QNR fractions whose dual chain has a specific long shape.
why: The dual picture (long chains of 2's and a few larger entries) is where Zaremba-type 'bounded digits' tools live. ES₅ becomes 'some QNR has a dual with ≤ 3 non-2 blocks'.
first_step: Express ES₅ via the dual: QNR B with p/B = [[2,…,2, a, 2,…,2, b, 2,…]] of a specific block shape; count such B via digit-structure.

title: Hyperbolic orbifold coverings: Riemann–Hurwitz between ES triangle orbifolds of different n
connection: If S²(x,y,z) covers S²(x′,y′,z′) with degree d, then χ scales: (4/n − 1) = d(4/n′ − 1). Orbifold coverings between triangle orbifolds (Singerman's list of inclusions of triangle groups) therefore give transport between n and n′.
why: Singerman's classification of triangle-group inclusions is finite and explicit, which might give a small set of exact transport laws.
first_step: From Singerman's list, derive all relations n ↦ n′ induced by inclusions Δ(x,y,z) ⊂ Δ(x′,y′,z′); check whether any maps primes to primes.
refs: Singerman, Finitely maximal Fuchsian groups (J. LMS 1972)

title: Lattice of ES solutions under scaling: the 'primitive' solution poset and Möbius inversion over n
connection: Solutions for n give solutions for kn by scaling, and GEOMETRY_ES: each primitive s gives exactly the multiples of m(s). So f(n) = Σ_{d | n} g(d), with g(d) = #{primitive s : m(s) = d}. ES at primes ⇔ g(p) > 0.
why: Möbius inversion makes 'primitive solutions at exactly p' the core object, and its Dirichlet series is the height zeta function restricted to primitive points.
first_step: Compute g(d) for d < 10⁵ and its Dirichlet series behaviour; check the size of g at primes vs composites.

title: Frobenius number analogue for three generators: n = tuv − u − v as a three-generator semigroup statistic?
connection: uv − u − v is the Frobenius number of ⟨u,v⟩. For three generators there are formulas (e.g. for ⟨u, v, w⟩ with structure, Rødseth). Is tuv − u − v the Frobenius number of a natural 3-generated semigroup (for instance ⟨u, v, tuv⟩ is trivial)? If so, I3 becomes 'every large n is a Frobenius number of a semigroup of a given shape'.
why: 'Which integers are Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups' is a studied question; a match would bring that literature in.
first_step: Search small cases: for given n = tuv − u − v, compute Frobenius numbers of ⟨a,b,c⟩ with a,b,c ≤ 50 and test whether some natural family reproduces tuv − u − v.

title: Conjugacy classes in SL₂(ℤ/4) and the slot lemma: '4 divides a pentagon entry' as a class condition on γ_w mod 4
connection: The slot lemma is a mod-4 condition on (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. on γ_w mod 4 together with the frieze. SL₂(ℤ/4) has order 48; the sign may be a class function on SL₂(ℤ/4) restricted to word images.
why: A class-function description would let representation theory of the finite group SL₂(ℤ/4) (and its Weil representation) organise all sign computations.
first_step: Tabulate γ_w mod 4 and mod 8 for all words of p < 10⁴; check whether the sign is a function of the conjugacy class (or of the double coset) mod 4 or 8.

title: Positive definite binary forms of discriminant −4(tp+1)… and the A/A* pairing as an ambiguous-form question
connection: Factorisations N = A·A* correspond to ambiguous forms/ideals of discriminant related to N. Words are factorisations with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t). Genus theory of disc −4N tells which ambiguous classes exist.
why: Gauss's genus theory counts factorisations as ambiguous classes, and the mod-t condition becomes a genus-character condition, a native class-group statement.
first_step: For small t, compute the genus characters of the ambiguous forms of disc −4N_t and identify which genus the word factorisations occupy.

title: Dirichlet's class number formula for Q(√−p) and the BM main term's L(1,χ) factors
connection: The BM main term involves L-values/class-number-type constants. Dirichlet's formula connects h(−4p) to L(1, χ_{−4p}). If the ES₅ main term at p contains L(1, χ_{−4p})-type factors, Siegel's theorem gives lower bounds (ineffectively) pointwise.
why: It is how class numbers enter pointwise theorems (Siegel). It would make the main term pointwise ≫ p^{−ε}, though only the main term, not the count.
first_step: Inspect BM_CORRECTED_COUNT / BOARD2_SLATE main-term formulas for p-dependent L-value factors; if present, apply Siegel/Burgess lower bounds.
